guides.title: Syntax — How Sentences Work
guides.summary: A complete account of sentence structure: how words group into phrases, how phrases nest into hierarchical trees, how verbs demand their arguments, why word order differs across languages, how questions and passives displace material, and what the constraints on all of this reveal about the human language faculty.

sections.heading: What Syntax Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: Syntax is the system that decides which strings of words count as sentences of a language and what those sentences mean structurally. It is not spelling, not punctuation, not vocabulary, and not the etiquette of formal writing. It is the largely unconscious machinery that lets a five-year-old who has never heard the sentence "the purple crocodile that ate my homework apologised twice" understand it instantly, and equally lets that child reject "crocodile the purple homework my ate that twice apologised" as not English at all. Neither string has ever been encountered before. Neither can be handled by memory. Something generative is at work. The central fact syntax exists to explain is often called discrete infinity: a finite brain, a finite vocabulary of perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 words for an educated adult, and a finite set of rules, yet an unbounded set of possible sentences. You can always insert one more adjective, one more relative clause, one more "I think that". There is no longest sentence in English in the way there is no largest integer. This rules out any account of language as a list of memorised expressions, and forces an account in terms of combination — small pieces assembled by rules into larger pieces, recursively. The second central fact is that meaning depends on structure, not merely on order. Consider "the police shot the rioters with rifles". If the rifles belong to the police, they are the instrument of shooting; if they belong to the rioters, they merely describe who was shot. The words are identical and in identical order. Only the invisible grouping differs. This is structural ambiguity, and it is the single most persuasive demonstration that sentences have hidden architecture. Every reader resolves such sentences constantly without noticing. A third fact is that syntactic knowledge is largely tacit. Native speakers can judge, with speed and striking agreement, that "who did you say that left?" is bad while "who did you say left?" is fine, yet almost none can state the rule involved. Linguists therefore treat grammaticality judgements as data about the mind, much as a physicist treats meter readings as data about the world, marking unacceptable strings with an asterisk. The judgements are noisy at the margins and vary by dialect, and there is genuine ongoing debate about how reliable introspective judgements are compared with large corpus counts or controlled acceptability experiments; the honest position is that all three sources are used and mostly converge. Why does this matter practically? Because syntax underlies every technology that processes language, every account of how children acquire speech, every clinical description of aphasia after stroke, every translation problem, and every serious attempt to write clearly. Understanding structure turns "this sentence feels wrong" into a diagnosis you can act on.

sections.heading: Constituents — Finding the Groups Inside a Sentence
sections.body: The foundational move in syntax is discovering that a sentence is not a flat chain of words but a nested set of groups called constituents. A constituent is any stretch of words that behaves as a single unit for the purposes of the grammar. In "the old dog on the porch barked loudly", the words "the old dog on the porch" form one unit, and "barked loudly" another; "dog on the" is not a unit at all, even though the words are adjacent. Constituency is not decided by intuition alone. Linguists use a battery of diagnostic tests, and a string that passes several of them is almost certainly a genuine constituent. The substitution test replaces a candidate string with a single pro-form: "the old dog on the porch" can be replaced by "it", and the sentence survives, whereas nothing can replace "dog on the". The movement or topicalisation test fronts the string: "on the porch, the old dog barked" is fine, so "on the porch" is a unit. The coordination test conjoins the candidate with a like element using "and": "the old dog on the porch and the cat in the window barked" works, so each conjunct is a constituent. The question-answer or fragment test asks whether the string can stand alone as an answer: to "what barked?" you may reply "the old dog on the porch", which is a full and natural fragment, but you may not reply "dog on the". The clefting test embeds the string in "it was ___ that ...": "it was the old dog on the porch that barked" is grammatical. These tests are tools, not oracles, and they sometimes disagree. Some genuine constituents resist movement; some non-constituents can be coordinated in special elliptical constructions such as "John gave Mary a book and Bill a record", where "Bill a record" is not obviously a unit under classical assumptions. Such cases are actively debated and have driven whole theoretical frameworks. The practical rule is convergence: if three or four independent tests agree, treat the string as a constituent. The reason constituency matters so much is that all further syntactic statements are stated over constituents. Rules do not refer to "the third word" or "everything before the verb"; they refer to "the subject noun phrase" or "the complement clause". Structure-dependence, as it is called, is one of the most robust findings in the field: no known human language forms questions by, say, reversing the linear order of words or fronting the fourth word. Instead, operations target structural units. Children appear to assume this from the start, rarely producing errors that would follow from a purely linear rule, which has been taken as evidence that structure-dependence is not learned from data but built into the architecture of the language faculty — a claim that remains contested but that no competing account has fully dissolved.

sections.heading: Phrases and Heads — the Architecture Every Phrase Shares
sections.body: Constituents come in types, and each type is organised around one obligatory word called the head. Before the head can be identified, its word class must be, and here traditional definitions fail badly. A noun is not "a person, place or thing" — "destruction", "arrival" and "honesty" are nouns denoting events and properties — and a verb is not "an action word", since "own", "cost" and "resemble" denote no action. Syntax defines classes distributionally, by where a word can occur: a noun is what can follow a determiner, pluralise and head a subject; a verb is what can carry tense and follow "must"; an adjective is what can sit between a determiner and a noun and take "very". Alongside these open classes sit small closed classes — determiners, auxiliaries, complementisers, conjunctions, prepositions — that carry the structural skeleton, are enormously frequent ("the" alone is about 6 percent of running English text), and are disproportionately lost in agrammatic aphasia. The head determines the category and much of the behaviour of the whole phrase. In the noun phrase "the enormous crate of overripe mangoes", the head is "crate": the phrase refers to a crate, it takes singular agreement because "crate" is singular ("the crate of mangoes is heavy", not "are heavy"), In "walked slowly toward the river", the head is the verb "walked". In "extremely fond of jazz", the head is the adjective "fond". In "just after midnight", the head is the preposition "after". A phrase is named for its head: noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, prepositional phrase, usually abbreviated NP, VP, AP, PP. Around the head, three structural positions recur so consistently across categories and across languages that they were generalised into a template known as X-bar theory, developed in the late 1960s and 1970s. Written with X standing for any category, the schema says a phrase XP consists of a specifier plus an intermediate projection X-bar, which in turn consists of the head plus its complements, with adjuncts attaching to X-bar. The vocabulary matters less than the three-way distinction it encodes. The complement is the phrase the head selects and is closest to it: "of overripe mangoes" completes "crate", "the river" completes "toward", "of jazz" completes "fond". Complements are typically obligatory or strongly expected, they sit adjacent to the head, and there is normally only one. Adjuncts are optional modifiers that can stack indefinitely: "the crate of mangoes in the hold from Manila that we bought yesterday". You can pile adjuncts on freely, and they generally attach outside complements, which is why "the crate in the hold of mangoes" sounds wrong. The specifier is the outermost element, typically one per phrase: the determiner "the" for nouns, "extremely" for the adjective, and in classical accounts the subject for the verb phrase. This uniformity matters because the child need not learn a separate blueprint for each category: learn that phrases have heads, complements, adjuncts and specifiers, and only a few parameters remain to be fixed per language — chiefly whether heads precede their complements, as in English and Swahili, or follow them, as in Japanese and Turkish.

sections.heading: Trees, Hierarchy and Structural Ambiguity
sections.body: Once constituents and heads are established, a sentence can be drawn as a tree: a diagram in which the whole sentence sits at the top, branches divide into its immediate constituents, and those divide again until individual words are reached at the bottom. Equivalently the structure can be written with labelled brackets, so "the dog chased a cat" becomes [S [NP the dog] [VP chased [NP a cat]]]. Trees are not decoration. They encode three claims simultaneously: which words group together, what category each group is, and which groups are inside which others. The vocabulary of trees is worth learning because syntactic rules are stated in it. A node immediately above another dominates it; a node above at any distance dominates it too. Two nodes with the same mother are sisters. The relation that does most of the work is c-command, introduced by Tanya Reinhart in 1976: a node c-commands its sisters and everything inside them. C-command turns out to be the relation that governs pronoun reference, negative polarity licensing, and quantifier scope, which is a striking result — several apparently unrelated phenomena all turn out to obey the same structural condition. Structural ambiguity is the clearest empirical payoff. "Visiting relatives can be tiresome" has two structures: one where "visiting" is a verb and "relatives" its object, meaning that going to see them is tiresome, and one where "visiting" modifies "relatives", meaning that relatives who visit are tiresome. "I saw the man with the telescope" attaches the prepositional phrase either to the verb phrase, giving the instrument reading, or to the noun phrase, giving the reading where the man possesses the telescope. "Old men and women" either has "old" scoping over both nouns or only over "men". Newspaper headlines exploit this accidentally with famous results: "British left waffles on Falklands", "Squad helps dog bite victim", "Complaints about NBA referees growing ugly". Attachment ambiguity has measurable psychological consequences. Reading-time experiments show that readers systematically prefer certain attachments, and that violating the preference costs measurable milliseconds and sometimes causes conscious breakdown. The best-known example is the garden-path sentence: "the horse raced past the barn fell" is fully grammatical — the horse that was raced past the barn fell — but almost every reader initially parses "raced" as the main verb and crashes at "fell". Others include "the old man the boats" and "the cotton clothing is made of grows in Mississippi". These sentences show that the parser commits to a structure incrementally, word by word, rather than waiting for the end. Ambiguity also compounds combinatorially. A sentence with n prepositional phrases in sequence has a number of possible attachment structures given by the Catalan numbers: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132. "I saw the man in the park with the telescope on the hill" has 14 parses in principle. Human listeners almost never notice, because context, plausibility and prosody prune the space instantly — but any computer parser must confront the full explosion, which is why statistical disambiguation became the central problem of computational syntax.

sections.heading: Subjects, Objects and Grammatical Functions
sections.body: Constituent structure tells you how words group; grammatical functions tell you what role each group plays. The main functions are subject, direct object, indirect object, predicative complement and oblique. These are relational notions — a noun phrase is not intrinsically a subject, it is the subject of a particular clause — and they cut across both structure and meaning. In English the subject is identified by a cluster of properties rather than a single one. It normally precedes the verb in declaratives; it inverts with the auxiliary in questions ("has she left?"); it controls verb agreement ("she walks" versus "they walk"); it appears in nominative form if it is a pronoun ("she", not "her"); it is the understood subject of an infinitive ("she wants to leave"); and it is the element that a tag question echoes ("she left, didn't she?"). Applying several of these tests together handles awkward cases. In "there are three problems", the tests point to "there" as the grammatical subject even though "three problems" carries the meaning and, oddly, controls the agreement — a genuine mismatch that theories handle in different ways. The direct object is the phrase that follows the verb without a preposition, becomes the subject under passivisation, and appears in accusative case for pronouns. This last diagnostic is nearly invisible in English, which marks case only on seven pronoun pairs (I/me, he/him, she/her, we/us, they/them, who/whom, and the vestigial thou/thee). Languages with rich case morphology make functions explicit on the noun itself: Latin, Russian, Finnish, Turkish and Hungarian all mark subject and object distinctly, and consequently permit far freer word order, because the case ending rather than the position identifies the role. Finnish has around fifteen cases; Hungarian is usually counted at eighteen; Latin uses six. It is essential to keep grammatical function separate from semantic role. In "the window broke", "the window" is the subject but semantically the thing affected, not an agent. In "the key opened the door", "the key" is subject but instrument. In "Sandra received a letter", she is subject but recipient. Conversely, in the passive "the door was opened by the key", the same instrument appears in an oblique phrase. Function and role are systematically related but not identical, and much of syntactic theory concerns exactly how one maps onto the other. Languages also differ in how they align these categories. English and most European languages are nominative-accusative: the single argument of an intransitive verb is treated like the agent of a transitive one. Ergative-absolutive languages, including Basque, Dyirbal, Georgian in some tenses, and many Mayan languages, treat the single intransitive argument like the object of a transitive verb instead, marking the transitive agent specially. Roughly a quarter of the world's languages show ergative patterning somewhere in their grammar, often only in certain tenses or only in the morphology and not the syntax — so-called split ergativity.

sections.heading: Verbs and Their Arguments — Valency and Theta Roles
sections.body: The verb is the organising centre of the clause, and its most consequential property is valency: how many arguments it requires and of what kind. "Sleep" is intransitive and takes one argument, the sleeper. "Devour" is transitive and requires two: "she devoured the pie", never "*she devoured". "Give" is ditransitive and requires three: giver, thing given, recipient. "Put" requires three of a different shape: agent, theme and location, and refuses to do without the location, which is why "*I put the book" is impossible where "*I gave the book" is merely elliptical. Each argument is assigned a semantic role, often called a theta role or thematic role. The standard inventory includes agent, the deliberate instigator; patient or theme, the entity affected or moved; experiencer, the one who perceives or feels; recipient and goal; source; instrument; beneficiary; and location. A widely assumed principle, the theta criterion in Chomskyan work, holds that each argument receives exactly one role and each role is assigned to exactly one argument. This immediately explains why "*she devoured the pie the cake" is ungrammatical: there is no second role available for the extra noun phrase. Verbs also select the syntactic category of their complements, a property called subcategorisation, and this is independent of theta roles. "Wonder" takes a question complement ("she wondered whether it rained") but not a noun phrase ("*she wondered the rain"). "Doubt" takes both. "Seem" takes a clause or an adjective but not a bare noun phrase. "Persuade" takes an object plus an infinitive ("persuade her to go"), while "promise" takes the same surface shape but assigns the infinitive's subject differently — in "she promised him to go", the goer is she, whereas in "she persuaded him to go" the goer is him. Children reliably misinterpret "promise" until around age six, a finding from Carol Chomsky's 1969 work that has been replicated many times. The same verb often permits several frames, and the alternations are systematic rather than random. The dative alternation pairs "give the book to Mary" with "give Mary the book", but it is restricted by an odd morphological condition: native Germanic verbs alternate freely, Latinate ones resist, so "tell her the news" is fine while "*explain her the news" is not for most speakers. The causative alternation pairs "the ice melted" with "the sun melted the ice", and applies to verbs of change of state but not to "*the pie devoured". The locative alternation pairs "load hay onto the wagon" with "load the wagon with hay", and the two differ in meaning: the second implies the wagon is full, an effect called the holistic interpretation. Learning these idiosyncratic restrictions poses a genuine puzzle, since children rarely receive explicit correction, and it remains one of the liveliest debates in acquisition research.

sections.heading: Word Order — Typology and the Head Parameter
sections.body: Given a subject, a verb and an object, there are six logically possible orders, and the world's languages are distributed among them with striking unevenness. Drawing on the World Atlas of Language Structures survey of over 1,300 languages, subject-object-verb order accounts for roughly 41 percent and subject-verb-object for roughly 35 percent, together covering about three-quarters of the sample. Verb-subject-object accounts for around 7 percent, found in Irish, Welsh, Classical Arabic and Māori. The three orders that place the object before the subject are vanishingly rare: verb-object-subject about 2 percent, object-verb-subject and object-subject-verb well under 1 percent each, the latter attested in a handful of Amazonian languages such as Warao and Nadëb. A further 14 percent or so have no dominant order at all. The overwhelming preference for subject-first is one of the few near- universals of human language and is usually attributed to a cognitive preference for mentioning the agent or topic first. Order correlations, first systematised by Joseph Greenberg in his 1963 paper on universals, are more revealing than raw frequencies. Verb-final languages overwhelmingly have postpositions rather than prepositions, place genitives before nouns, put relative clauses before their head nouns, and place auxiliaries after main verbs. Verb-initial and verb-medial languages show the mirror image. Japanese illustrates the package: "Tarō ga hon o katta" is literally Taro-subject book-object bought, with the verb last, postpositions, and prenominal relative clauses. English illustrates the opposite package almost perfectly. The head-directionality parameter explains the clustering economically: fix whether heads precede or follow their complements and dozens of surface facts fall out at once. This is elegant, and it makes acquisition tractable — the child needs only a few unambiguous examples to set the switch. But the generalisation is imperfect. German is verb-final in subordinate clauses and verb-second in main clauses. Persian is verb-final yet has prepositions. Mandarin has prepositions and postpositions and mixes the correlations freely. Contemporary work therefore treats head-direction as a strong statistical tendency with real explanatory force rather than an exceptionless law, and alternative explanations in terms of processing efficiency — minimising the distance between words that depend on each other, a principle called dependency length minimisation — account for much of the same data without invoking an innate parameter. Even languages with free order are not truly free. Russian permits all six orders of a simple transitive clause, but they are not interchangeable: they differ in what is presented as given information and what as new. Order in such languages encodes information structure — topic, focus, contrast — rather than grammatical role, which the case endings already supply. The general principle, sometimes called the given-before-new preference, appears in every language studied.

sections.heading: Movement — Why Words Turn Up Far From Where They Belong
sections.body: Many sentences contain an element that is interpreted in one position but pronounced in another. In "which book did Sarah read?", "which book" is understood as the object of "read", the position after the verb, yet it appears at the front. The gap after "read" is real: you cannot fill it, since "*which book did Sarah read it?" is ungrammatical in standard English. Syntacticians describe this as movement, or displacement, and represent the vacated position as a trace or copy. Movement operations fall into a few well-defined types. Wh-movement fronts an interrogative or relative phrase, as in questions and relative clauses. Subject-auxiliary inversion moves the finite auxiliary in front of the subject, which is why "she has left" becomes "has she left?" and why English inserts a dummy "do" when there is no auxiliary available — "did she leave?" — a construction called do-support that emerged in English between roughly 1400 and 1700 and is typologically unusual. Head movement raises a verb to a higher functional position, which explains why French verbs precede adverbs ("Jean mange souvent des pommes", John eats often apples) while English verbs follow them ("John often eats apples"). Passivisation moves the object to subject position, leaving the agent optionally expressed in a "by" phrase. Raising moves a subject out of an embedded clause: "Susan seems to be tired" has Susan interpreted as the subject of "be tired", not of "seem", which is why "there seems to be a problem" and "it seems to be raining" are possible with semantically empty subjects. The evidence for movement rather than plain base generation is substantial and largely indirect. It comes from the strict complementary distribution of filler and gap, from agreement effects computed at the original site, from the fact that idiom chunks survive displacement ("the cat seems to be out of the bag"), and from reconstruction effects where a fronted phrase is interpreted as though still low in the tree. Displacement can span unbounded distance. "Which book did you say that Mary believed that John claimed that Susan had read?" is comprehensible although the gap is four clauses deep. This long-distance dependency is one of the strongest arguments that grammar cannot be a simple finite-state device: no machine that tracks only a bounded amount of context can match arbitrarily distant fillers with their gaps. Chomsky's 1956 demonstration of this point, using centre-embedded constructions such as "the rat the cat the dog chased killed ate the malt", was foundational for both linguistics and computer science. Not every framework accepts movement literally. Head-driven phrase structure grammar and lexical functional grammar handle the same facts with feature-passing mechanisms, in which a "slash" feature records an unfilled requirement and is transmitted down the tree until discharged at the gap. Empirically these approaches are largely equivalent for the core cases; they differ in what they predict at the margins and in how naturally they extend to processing models. The disagreement is genuine, decades old and unresolved.

sections.heading: Agreement, Concord and Features
sections.body: Agreement is the requirement that two elements share the value of some grammatical feature. English retains only a threadbare system: present-tense verbs agree with their subject in person and number, visible almost entirely as the third-person singular "-s", plus the richer paradigm of "be" with its am, is, are, was, were. Demonstratives agree in number ("this book", "these books"). That is nearly the whole of it, which is why English speakers find agreement in other languages laborious. Many languages agree far more extensively. Spanish and Italian verbs distinguish six person-number combinations in each tense, so the subject pronoun becomes redundant and is usually dropped — the pro-drop or null-subject property. Bantu languages such as Swahili require every element of a noun phrase to carry a prefix matching the noun's class, of which Swahili has around fifteen, so "watoto wawili wazuri wamefika" marks the class on the numeral, the adjective and the verb alike. Hungarian and Basque agree with the object as well as the subject; Georgian verbs may agree with three arguments at once, producing verb forms that encode a whole clause. The mechanism is generally described in terms of features that are valued and copied. The subject carries interpretable person and number; the verb enters with those features unvalued; a syntactic operation matches them under c-command and copies the values. The reason this is stated structurally rather than linearly is that agreement systematically ignores intervening material: "the box of apples is heavy" agrees with "box", not the closer "apples", because "box" is the structural head. Speakers do make errors here, and the pattern of errors is informative. Attraction errors — "the key to the cabinets are missing" — occur reliably in production experiments at rates of several percent, rising when the intervening noun is plural and when it is closer to the verb. This is one of the cleanest demonstrations that the production system is structurally organised but imperfectly buffered. Notional agreement complicates the picture in ways that are genuinely unsettled rather than simply wrong. British English commonly treats collective nouns as plural when the members act individually ("the committee are divided"), where American English prefers singular. "None" has been used with both singular and plural verbs since the ninth century, despite a persistent prescriptive myth that it must be singular. Coordinated subjects joined by "or" typically agree with the nearer conjunct. Singular "they", attested in Chaucer and Shakespeare and now standard for an individual of unspecified or non-binary gender, takes plural verb forms but singular reference, which is exactly the pattern already found in singular "you". None of this is decay; all of it is ordinary variation in a system where semantics and morphology can pull in different directions.

sections.heading: Clauses Inside Clauses — Subordination, Coordination and Recursion
sections.body: The property that most sharply distinguishes human syntax from animal signalling is recursion: a clause can contain another clause of the same type, without any principled limit. "Bill knows that Mary said that John thinks that it will rain" nests four clauses. This is what generates discrete infinity, and it is why grammars are written as rule systems rather than as inventories. Subordinate clauses come in three broad functional types. Complement clauses serve as arguments of a verb, noun or adjective, typically introduced by "that", "whether", "if" or "for": "she believes that the bridge is safe", "the claim that the bridge is safe", "eager for the bridge to be safe". Relative clauses modify a noun and contain a gap corresponding to it: "the bridge that engineers inspected ___". English distinguishes restrictive relatives, which narrow reference and take no commas, from non-restrictive ones, which add parenthetical information and are set off by commas and by a distinct intonation contour. Adverbial clauses modify the whole clause and specify time, cause, condition, concession or purpose: "when the tide fell", "because the bolts had corroded", "although nobody noticed". Coordination differs fundamentally from subordination. Coordinated elements are of equal rank, joined by "and", "or", "but", "nor" or "yet", and must generally be of like category — the coordinate structure requirement that generates the stylistic advice about parallelism. Coordination also permits ellipsis of shared material, giving gapping ("John ordered soup and Mary ___ salad"), right-node raising ("John cooked and Mary ate the fish"), and verb-phrase ellipsis ("John left before Mary did ___"). Recursion has a hard practical limit that is not grammatical but psychological. Centre-embedded relatives become unparseable after two levels: "the rat the cat chased died" is difficult, and "the rat the cat the dog bit chased died" is essentially impossible to process despite being perfectly grammatical by the rules. Right-branching recursion causes no such trouble: "this is the dog that chased the cat that killed the rat that ate the malt" can continue indefinitely. The asymmetry is strong evidence for a distinction between competence, the underlying knowledge, and performance, what memory and attention permit — a distinction Chomsky drew in 1965 and which remains one of the field's load-bearing assumptions, though critics argue it too easily excuses a theory from awkward data. Whether recursion is truly universal became a heated controversy after Daniel Everett argued in 2005 that Pirahã, spoken by a few hundred people in the Brazilian Amazon, lacks clausal embedding altogether, using parataxis instead. The claim has been disputed on both descriptive and theoretical grounds and is not settled. What is agreed is that even if one language lacked recursion, the capacity for it is present in every other, and that some form of hierarchical combination is indispensable.

sections.heading: Binding — Who Can Refer to Whom
sections.body: Pronouns and reflexives look simple and are governed by a surprisingly intricate structural system. Compare "John washed himself" with "John said that Mary washed himself". The second is impossible, though nothing about meaning forbids it. Compare "John washed him", where "him" must be someone other than John, with "John said that Mary washed him", where "him" may be John. The pattern is systematic across speakers and across many languages, and it is not learned by correction. The classical account, binding theory, was formulated by Noam Chomsky in Lectures on Government and Binding in 1981 and consists of three conditions. Principle A: an anaphor — a reflexive such as "himself" or a reciprocal such as "each other" — must be bound within its local domain, roughly its own clause. Principle B: a pronoun must be free, that is not bound, within that same local domain. Principle C: a full referring expression such as a proper name must be free everywhere, which explains why "he thinks John is clever" cannot have "he" refer to John, while "John thinks he is clever" can. "Bound" is defined structurally, using c-command: a node binds another if it c-commands it and shares its reference index. C-command, not linear precedence, is the operative relation, and the evidence is neat. In "the mother of John admires himself", "John" precedes the reflexive but is buried inside a prepositional phrase and so does not c-command it; the sentence is bad. In "John's mother admires herself", the reflexive correctly takes the c-commanding "John's mother". Quantifier binding shows the same asymmetry: "every boy loves his mother" allows the distributive reading where each boy loves his own mother, but "his mother loves every boy" does not, because the quantifier no longer c-commands the pronoun. Cross-linguistic variation is substantial and has driven decades of refinement. Many languages have long-distance reflexives that may take an antecedent several clauses away: Chinese "ziji", Japanese "zibun", Icelandic "sig" and Korean "caki" all do this, usually with the added constraint that the antecedent must be a subject, and often with a further requirement that it be the perspective-holder of the sentence. Some languages, including Norwegian and Russian, distinguish possessive reflexives that must refer to the subject from ordinary possessives that must not. Logophoric pronouns in several West African languages, notably Ewe, are dedicated forms used only for the person whose speech or thought is being reported. These facts complicate the simple three-principle picture considerably, and no fully general theory commands consensus. Many researchers now think binding is not a single module but the interaction of structural locality with discourse-level perspective. What is not in doubt is the core observation: the possibilities for pronoun reference are constrained by hierarchical structure in ways that no account based on word order or meaning alone can reproduce.

sections.heading: Islands — The Limits on What Can Be Extracted
sections.body: Although displacement can cross unbounded distance, it cannot cross just anything. Certain constituents behave as syntactic islands: material inside them cannot be extracted. John Robert Ross identified the main cases in his 1967 dissertation, and they remain among the most robust generalisations in the field precisely because they are so unlikely to be learned from experience. The complex noun phrase constraint blocks extraction out of a clause inside a noun phrase. From "you believed the claim that Susan read the book" you cannot ask "*what did you believe the claim that Susan read?" even though the corresponding question without the noun, "what did you believe that Susan read?", is perfect. The relative clause version is equally sharp: "*which book did you meet the man who wrote?" The subject condition blocks extraction from a subject: "*which candidate did supporters of ___ riot?" is bad, while extraction from an object is fine — "you saw supporters of the candidate" yields "which candidate did you see supporters of?" The adjunct condition blocks extraction from adverbial clauses: "*what did John leave because Mary bought?" The coordinate structure constraint blocks extraction from one conjunct only: "*what did John eat beans and?" But extraction from all conjuncts simultaneously, called across-the-board extraction, is fine — "what did John cook and Mary eat?" The wh-island constraint degrades extraction across another wh-phrase: "?what do you wonder who bought?" is markedly worse than "what do you think Bill bought?" Islands matter for three reasons. First, they are near-universal, appearing with only mild variation across typologically unrelated languages, though the strength varies — Scandinavian languages permit extraction from some relative clauses that English blocks, and Japanese, which forms questions without movement, shows much weaker effects. Second, the negative evidence needed to learn them is essentially absent from a child's input; children do not produce island violations and are not corrected for them, which makes islands a favourite argument for innate constraints. Third, they force any theory to say something about locality: extraction must proceed in short steps through designated escape hatches, and islands are the configurations that lack one. There is a serious alternative account, and it deserves to be stated fairly. Processing-based theories argue that island effects arise from the difficulty of holding a filler in memory while entering a structurally complex, low-salience or discourse-backgrounded domain. Evidence for this includes gradient acceptability rather than sharp categorical judgements, sensitivity to lexical choice and to the number of extractions, and the fact that some island violations improve dramatically with better context or with a resumptive pronoun ("this is the man who I can't remember whether he came"). Jon Sprouse and colleagues have argued from experimental data that individual differences in working memory do not predict island sensitivity, which cuts against the pure processing account. The debate is live and empirical, and a careful reader should hold both accounts in view rather than choosing a side prematurely.

sections.heading: Rival Frameworks — Different Ways to Draw the Same Facts
sections.body: The phrase-structure trees described in most textbooks come from one tradition, the generative programme launched by Chomsky's Syntactic Structures in 1957 and developed through the Standard Theory, Government and Binding, and the Minimalist Program from 1995 onward. It is influential but not the only serious framework, and knowing the alternatives protects against mistaking one notation for reality. Dependency grammar, systematised by Lucien Tesnière in work published posthumously in 1959, dispenses with phrasal nodes entirely. Every word except one depends directly on another word, and the single independent word — normally the finite verb — is the root. "The dog chased a cat" becomes a graph where "chased" is root, "dog" and "cat" depend on it, "the" and "a" depend on those nouns. Dependency representations are compact, map straightforwardly onto languages with free word order, and have won the computational field: Universal Dependencies, launched in 2014, now provides consistently annotated dependency treebanks for over 100 languages, and most modern parsers output dependencies rather than constituents. Categorial grammar, going back to Kazimierz Ajdukiewicz in 1935 and developed as combinatory categorial grammar by Mark Steedman, treats syntax as a form of type calculus. A transitive verb has the category (S\NP)/NP, meaning "something that combines with a noun phrase on its right and then a noun phrase on its left to yield a sentence". Combination is function application, which yields an exceptionally tight link between syntax and semantics and handles coordination and extraction elegantly. Lexical functional grammar, developed by Joan Bresnan and Ronald Kaplan around 1982, splits the representation in two: a constituent structure capturing order and grouping, and a functional structure capturing subject, object and features. Head-driven phrase structure grammar, from Carl Pollard and Ivan Sag in 1987 and 1994, encodes everything in richly typed feature structures unified during derivation, with no movement operations at all. Both are non-transformational, both are computationally implementable, and both have large working grammars written in them. Construction grammar, associated with Charles Fillmore, Paul Kay and Adele Goldberg from the late 1980s, denies the sharp division between lexicon and rules. Its central claim is that form-and-meaning pairings exist at every level of generality, from single morphemes to idioms like "the more the merrier" to abstract patterns like the ditransitive, and that the abstract patterns themselves carry meaning independent of the verb. This explains why "she sneezed the napkin off the table" is interpretable despite "sneeze" being intransitive: the caused-motion construction supplies the meaning. These frameworks are not simply notational variants. They make different predictions about learning, about processing, and about which generalisations are accidental. But for the great majority of everyday descriptive work they converge, and a fact stated in one can usually be restated in another.

sections.heading: Parsing — Computing Structure in Minds and Machines
sections.body: Knowing a grammar is not the same as using it. Parsing is the process of recovering structure from a string in real time, and it is a distinct problem with its own constraints. Human parsing is incremental and predictive. Eye-tracking studies show that readers commit to structure within roughly 200 to 300 milliseconds of encountering a word, and self-paced reading shows measurable slowdowns of 30 to 100 milliseconds at points of syntactic difficulty. Two broad classes of theory compete. Serial models, notably the garden-path model of Lyn Frazier from 1978, propose that the parser builds one structure at a time using simple structural heuristics — minimal attachment, which prefers the tree with fewest nodes, and late closure, which attaches new material to the currently open phrase — and reanalyses only when the commitment fails. Constraint-based models, associated with Maryellen MacDonald and Michael Tanenhaus in the 1990s, propose that multiple structures are activated in parallel and weighted continuously by frequency, plausibility, context and prosody. The evidence is genuinely mixed; both capture parts of the data, and the field has not converged. Machine parsing has followed a different arc. Early systems used hand-written context-free grammars with algorithms such as the Cocke-Younger-Kasami chart parser, which runs in time proportional to the cube of sentence length, or Earley's algorithm from 1970. These broke on real text, because a grammar broad enough to cover naturally occurring sentences assigns thousands of parses to each one. The breakthrough was statistical: the Penn Treebank, released in 1993 with about 4.5 million words of hand-annotated Wall Street Journal text, allowed probabilistic context-free grammars to be estimated from data and the most likely parse selected. Accuracy on that benchmark climbed from roughly 75 percent labelled bracketing accuracy in the early 1990s to around 92 percent by 2010 with lexicalised and discriminative models. Transition-based dependency parsers, introduced by Joakim Nivre around 2003, changed the economics again: they process a sentence left to right in linear time using a stack and a sequence of shift and arc decisions, making them fast enough for web-scale use. Neural models from about 2014 onward, and then transformer-based systems, pushed dependency accuracy above 95 percent on English and made multilingual parsing practical. An important caveat: large language models produce fluent, largely grammatical text without any explicit parser or tree. This has been read by some as evidence that explicit syntax is unnecessary. That inference is too quick. Probing studies find that the internal representations of such models encode substantial hierarchical information, and the models still fail on precisely the constructions that stress structure — deep centre-embedding, long-distance agreement across intervening nouns, island violations. What the models demonstrate is that structure can be learned implicitly from enormous data; what they do not demonstrate is that structure is absent.

sections.heading: Acquisition, Variation and Change
sections.body: Children arrive at essentially adult syntax on a fast and remarkably uniform schedule. Single words appear around 12 months, two-word combinations around 18 to 24 months, and from about 24 to 36 months the productive grammar expands rapidly: auxiliaries, questions, negation, embedded clauses and passives all consolidate. By roughly four years, most core structures are in place, with a few late items — full passives, "promise"-type control, some relative clause types — settling by six or seven. The uniformity holds across languages, across wildly different amounts of child-directed speech, and across cultures where adults do not address infants directly at all. Children's errors are as informative as their successes, and the striking thing is which errors do not occur. English-speaking children overgeneralise morphology enthusiastically, saying "goed", "foots" and "he doed it", which shows they have extracted a rule rather than memorised forms. But they essentially never produce structure-independent errors such as forming a question by fronting the linearly first auxiliary: given "the man who is tall is happy", children do not say "*is the man who tall is happy?" Nor do they violate island constraints or binding principles. The gap between what a purely data-driven learner might plausibly try and what children actually try is the core of the argument from the poverty of the stimulus. That argument is contested and should be presented as such. Usage-based researchers, notably Michael Tomasello, argue that children build grammar gradually from item-specific schemas and that corpora contain more of the relevant evidence than the poverty argument allows. Computational learnability results cut both ways. The honest summary is that everyone agrees the outcome is uniform and rapid; the disagreement concerns how much structure must be presupposed to explain it. Syntax also changes over historical time, more slowly than vocabulary but unmistakably. English was verb-second in Old English much as German still is, and lost that property between roughly 1200 and 1500. Do-support arose in the same window. The modal auxiliaries "can", "may", "will" and "shall" were ordinary verbs in Old English and became a distinct functional class by the sixteenth century. Grammaticalisation is the general mechanism: content words erode into function words along well-attested pathways — motion verbs into future markers, as with "going to" becoming "gonna"; demonstratives into definite articles; nouns meaning "body" into reflexives. The pathways are directional and cross-linguistically repeated, which suggests the process is driven by ordinary pressures of frequency, reanalysis by learners, and phonetic reduction rather than by anything language-specific. Synchronic variation works the same way: dialects differ syntactically, not merely in accent and vocabulary, and the differences are rule-governed. African American English has a habitual aspect marker, the invariant "be" of "he be working", which expresses recurrent activity, something no standard English form encodes, and contrasts with "he working" for the present moment. Many British dialects permit "I amn't"; Scots and the American South permit double modals such as "might could". Each is a systematic grammar with its own constraints, and its speakers make sharp judgements about what the dialect allows. Treating such systems as errors mistakes a social fact about prestige for a structural fact about grammar.

sections.heading: Prescription, Description and Diagnosing a Sentence That Has Gone Wrong
sections.body: It is worth separating two questions that get confused constantly. The descriptive question is what the rules of a language actually are, discovered by observing speakers. The prescriptive question is which variants are socially favoured in formal registers. Both are legitimate, but they answer to different evidence, and prescriptive rules with no descriptive basis have a well-documented history. The ban on split infinitives was invented in the nineteenth century by analogy with Latin, where the infinitive is a single word and cannot be split; English writers had split them since the fourteenth century. The ban on stranded prepositions traces to John Dryden in 1672 and has never described English usage. The insistence that "none" is singular, that "hopefully" cannot modify a clause, and that "they" cannot be singular are all similarly unfounded. Genuine formal-register conventions do exist — agreement, case in relative pronouns, parallelism in coordination — and being fluent means controlling registers, not obeying folklore. When a sentence genuinely fails, the fault is almost always structural and can be located by a short procedure.
steps: Find the finite verb of the main clause. If there is none, or if there are two competing for the same subject, the sentence is a fragment or a run-on and no amount of rewording the middle will fix it.

Identify that verb's subject by asking who or what performs or undergoes it, then check agreement against the head noun of the subject, not the nearest noun. In 'the box of rusted bolts were missing', the head is 'box', so the verb must be 'was'.
Check each argument the verb requires. A transitive verb with no object, or a verb like 'put' with no location, leaves a hole the reader will feel as incompleteness even if they cannot name it.

Trace every modifier to the word it attaches to and confirm that word is adjacent or unmistakable. Dangling modifiers arise when the implied subject of a participial phrase is not the sentence subject: 'having finished the report, the printer jammed' makes the printer the author.

Trace every pronoun to a single unambiguous antecedent that c-commands or precedes it in the discourse. If two candidates are available, the reader will pick the wrong one about half the time; replace the pronoun with the noun.
Check coordination for like categories. 'She likes hiking, to swim and old films' fails because the three conjuncts are a gerund, an infinitive and a noun phrase.
Count the levels of embedding between the subject and its verb. More than one centre-embedded clause will defeat most readers regardless of grammaticality; unpack it into two sentences.
Read the sentence aloud. Prosody and syntax are tightly coupled, and a place where your voice hesitates is almost always a place where the structure branches badly.

guides.title: Phonology — Sound Systems & Patterns
guides.summary: How languages organise speech sounds into systems: phonemes and contrast, allophones, distinctive features, syllables and phonotactics, stress, tone and intonation, the processes that reshape sounds in context, and the methods used to analyse an unfamiliar language.

sections.heading: What Phonology Studies
sections.body:
Every human language uses a small number of speech sounds to build an unlimited number of words, and every
language organises those sounds according to a system its speakers know without ever having been taught it.
Phonology is the study of that system. It asks not what noises the mouth can make, but which differences
between noises a particular language treats as meaningful, how those units combine, and what happens to
them when they meet.

The distinction between phonology and its sister discipline phonetics is the first thing to get straight,
because everything else depends on it. Phonetics is the physical science of speech: how the vocal tract
produces sound, what the acoustic waveform looks like, how the ear and brain decode it. It measures things
in milliseconds and hertz, and its findings are about human bodies in general. Phonology is about knowledge:
the abstract, language-specific patterning that sits above the physical detail. A phonetician can tell you
that the p in the English word pin is followed by roughly 60 milliseconds of aspiration, a puff of breath,
while the p in spin has almost none. A phonologist observes that English speakers hear both as the same
sound and cannot tell you the difference without training, whereas a speaker of Thai, Hindi or Korean hears
those two as sharply distinct sounds capable of distinguishing words. The physical facts are the same in
both cases. The systems built on top of them are not.

This is why phonology matters beyond the seminar room. It explains why a fluent second-language speaker
retains an accent for decades: the phonological system acquired in infancy filters incoming sound into
native categories, and distinctions that category system does not encode become genuinely hard to hear, not
merely hard to say. Japanese-speaking adults famously struggle with the English r and l contrast, not out
of any deficiency but because Japanese has a single liquid consonant occupying that acoustic region, so a
lifetime of listening has trained the perceptual system to treat that whole region as one thing. Infants at
six months can discriminate the contrasts of any language; by twelve months, that ability has narrowed to
the contrasts their ambient language uses. Phonology is the record of that narrowing.

The field also explains a great deal that speakers experience as intuition. Why does the plural of cat
sound like s but the plural of dog sound like z, though both are spelled with the same letter and no one
teaches the rule? Why does an English speaker instantly judge blick to be a possible word and bnick not
to be, despite having encountered neither? Why do foreign borrowings get reshaped, so that Japanese renders
the English word strike as sutoraiku? In each case a speaker is applying an unconscious system, and
recovering that system from its outputs is precisely what phonological analysis does.

sections.heading: The Phoneme: Contrast and Minimal Pairs
sections.body:
The foundational unit of phonology is the phoneme, and the cleanest definition of it is functional rather
than physical: a phoneme is a sound category that can distinguish one word from another in a given language.
It is not a sound but a contrast, a slot in a system, and it exists only relative to the language you are
describing. There is no universal inventory of phonemes that all languages draw from; there are only the
oppositions each language happens to exploit.

The workhorse method for establishing phonemes is the minimal pair: two words that differ in meaning and
differ in exactly one sound in the same position. English pat and bat differ only in the initial consonant
and mean different things, so p and b belong to different phonemes in English. Pat, pet, pit, pot and putt
differ only in the vowel, establishing five distinct vowel phonemes at a stroke. When a full minimal pair
cannot be found, because the vocabulary happens not to contain one, analysts fall back on near-minimal
pairs, where the surrounding material is closely comparable, and on the general logic of distribution.

What counts as one sound differing is itself a theoretical claim, and it is where the beginner most often
goes wrong. Minimal pairs must be judged by sound, not spelling. English through and threw are not a
minimal pair at all; they are homophones, identical in sound. Meanwhile knight and night differ in spelling
but not in sound. Spelling systems are historical artefacts, sometimes centuries out of date with
pronunciation, and treating them as evidence about phonology produces nonsense. This is why phonologists
write in the International Phonetic Alphabet, conventionally between slashes for phonemes and square
brackets for physical sounds.

The size of phoneme inventories varies dramatically and is one of the great facts of linguistic typology.
Rotokas, spoken in Bougainville, is often cited as having around eleven phonemes; Pirahã, in the Amazon,
is described with a comparably tiny inventory. At the other extreme, several Khoisan languages of southern
Africa run past a hundred, largely because they use click consonants combined with a rich set of secondary
articulations. Most languages fall between twenty and forty. English, depending on the variety and the
analyst, is usually given about twenty-four consonants and anywhere from eleven to twenty vowel phonemes,
the vowel count being where dialects diverge most.

Crucially, inventory size does not correlate with expressive power or complexity of the language overall. A
language with few phonemes typically compensates with longer words or richer syllable structure or tone.
Total communicative capacity appears roughly constant; the accounting simply happens in different places. A
Hawaiian word carrying the same information as an English one will generally have more syllables, because
each syllable carries fewer bits, and measured information rates across languages come out remarkably
similar despite enormous differences in the machinery used to achieve them.

sections.heading: Allophones: One Phoneme, Many Sounds
sections.body:
If a phoneme is a category, its members are allophones: the physically distinct sounds that a language
treats as the same thing. Recognising allophonic variation is the central analytic skill of phonology,
because speakers are systematically unaware of it in their own language while being acutely aware of it in
someone else's.

English provides a standard example in the phoneme p. At the start of a stressed syllable it is aspirated,
released with a burst of breath, as in pin. After s, as in spin, it is unaspirated. At the end of a word,
as in stop, it is frequently unreleased, the lips closing and simply staying closed. These are three
audibly different sounds. Yet no English word is distinguished by choosing between them, and native
speakers report hearing one sound. The three are allophones of a single phoneme.

Two relationships between allophones matter. The first is complementary distribution: each variant occurs
in environments where the others never do, so their contexts carve up the space without overlap, like two
actors who are never on stage at once and might therefore be the same actor. Aspirated and unaspirated p in
English are in complementary distribution, and the environments can be stated as a rule. The second is free
variation, where two variants may occur in the same environment without changing meaning, as when a speaker
releases or does not release the final t of cat. Free variation is genuinely optional, often socially or
stylistically conditioned, and it does not undermine the phonemic analysis.

The analytic procedure follows directly. Given a set of transcribed data, if two sounds ever contrast in
identical environments, they belong to different phonemes. If they never do, and their environments are
complementary, they are candidates for allophones of one phoneme. The analyst then asks which of the two is
the underlying form, the one stored in memory, and which is derived by rule. The usual criterion is
distributional: the variant with the wider or more general distribution, the one that appears in the
elsewhere case, is taken as basic, and the restricted variant is derived. In English, unaspirated p appears
in a specific set of environments while aspirated p appears in another, but the analysis usually takes the
plain segment as basic and aspiration as added, partly because aspiration is an added phonetic property and
partly because that direction yields the simpler rule.

The same physical sound can occupy different roles in different systems, which is the deepest lesson here.
The sounds written ph and p in Hindi are separate phonemes, distinguishing words, so an English speaker's
automatic aspiration can change a Hindi word's meaning. Meanwhile the English distinction between the
sounds at the ends of bath and bathe is phonemic in English but merely allophonic in Spanish, where the two
appear in complementary environments. There is no fact about a sound in isolation that tells you its status;
status is always relative to a system.

sections.heading: Distinctive Features: Taking Sounds Apart
sections.body:
Phonemes behave in ways that would be inexplicable if they were unanalysable wholes. Rules apply not to
random collections of sounds but to natural classes: all the nasals, all the voiceless stops, all the front
vowels. This observation drove the development of distinctive feature theory, which treats each phoneme as
a bundle of smaller properties, and it is one of the most productive ideas in twentieth-century linguistics.

Roman Jakobson, working with Gunnar Fant and Morris Halle in the late 1940s and early 1950s, proposed that
a small universal set of binary features, each defined acoustically, could characterise every contrast in
every language. Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle's 1968 book The Sound Pattern of English, universally
abbreviated SPE, recast the features in largely articulatory terms and made them the currency of generative
phonology. A feature is written with a plus or minus value: the sound b is [+voice], [−nasal], [−continuant],
[+labial]; the sound s is [−voice], [+continuant], [+coronal], [+strident].

Features do real explanatory work. Consider a rule that turns the English plural ending into an s after
p, t, k, f and the th of both, and into a z after b, d, g, v, m, n, l, r and vowels. Listed as segments,
that is arbitrary. Stated in features it is a single fact: the ending agrees in voicing with the preceding
sound, and the first list is exactly the set of voiceless obstruents. A rule that must list eight segments
to do what one feature does is almost certainly the wrong analysis. This evaluation metric, that the correct
rule is the shorter one in feature terms, was a central methodological claim of SPE.

The major feature dimensions are worth knowing. Major class features separate consonants from vowels and
distinguish obstruents from sonorants: [consonantal], [sonorant], [syllabic]. Manner features describe how
airflow is shaped: [continuant] for whether airflow is blocked, [nasal] for velum lowering, [lateral] for
airflow round the sides of the tongue, [strident] for noisy high-frequency friction. Laryngeal features
describe the vocal folds: [voice], [spread glottis] which covers aspiration, [constricted glottis] which
covers glottalisation and ejectives. Place features describe where the constriction is: [labial],
[coronal], [dorsal], with sub-features like [anterior] and [distributed] refining coronal place.

Later work reorganised features into a hierarchy rather than a flat list. Feature geometry, developed in the
1980s by researchers including George Clements, arranges features on a tree so that a rule can target a
whole node, explaining why all place features tend to spread together in assimilation while voicing spreads
independently. There is genuine ongoing disagreement about whether features are innate and universal, as
the classical position holds, or emergent from the phonetics of the particular language, as more recent
usage-based approaches argue. The evidence does not currently settle it.

sections.heading: Consonant Systems
sections.body:
Consonants are sounds made with a significant constriction somewhere in the vocal tract, and describing one
traditionally requires three coordinates: where the constriction is, how airflow is obstructed, and what
the vocal folds are doing. This three-way description, place, manner and voicing, will identify almost any
consonant well enough to find it on a chart.

Place of articulation runs from the lips backward. Bilabial sounds join the two lips, as in p, b, m.
Labiodental sounds put the lower lip against the upper teeth, as in f and v. Dental sounds place the tongue
tip at or between the teeth, as in the th of thin. Alveolar sounds contact the ridge behind the upper
teeth: t, d, n, s, z, l. Postalveolar sounds sit slightly further back, as in the sh of ship. Retroflex
sounds curl the tongue tip back, common in the languages of South Asia. Palatal sounds raise the tongue
body to the hard palate. Velar sounds contact the soft palate: k, g, and the ng of sing. Uvular sounds
engage the uvula, as in the standard French r. Pharyngeal sounds constrict the throat, prominent in Arabic
and Hebrew. Glottal sounds are made at the vocal folds themselves, including the h of hat and the glottal
stop.

Manner of articulation describes the degree and kind of obstruction. Stops or plosives close the tract
completely and release it. Fricatives narrow it enough to produce turbulent noise. Affricates begin as a
stop and release into a fricative, as in the ch of church. Nasals close the oral tract but lower the velum
so air escapes through the nose. Approximants narrow the tract without turbulence, including l, r, w and y.
Trills and taps involve one or several rapid contacts, as in the Spanish rr and r respectively.

Voicing is whether the vocal folds vibrate during the constriction. Many languages contrast voiced and
voiceless pairs. But voicing is really shorthand for a more precise phonetic quantity, voice onset time,
the interval between the release of a stop and the start of vocal fold vibration. Languages carve that
continuum differently: English contrasts roughly zero VOT with about 60 milliseconds of aspiration, Spanish
contrasts prevoicing of around minus 80 milliseconds with roughly zero, and Thai uses three regions of the
same continuum. The labels voiced and voiceless can therefore mean different physical things in different
languages, a fact that causes constant confusion in language teaching.

Some consonant types recur cross-linguistically and some are rare. Nearly every language has stops at
labial, coronal and dorsal places, and nearly every language has nasals and at least one fricative, usually
s. Clicks, ejectives and implosives are geographically clustered rather than randomly distributed. The
strong tendencies here, described by Joseph Greenberg and others as implicational universals, take the form:
if a language has X it will also have Y. If a language has voiced fricatives, it has voiceless ones.

sections.heading: Vowel Systems
sections.body:
Vowels are produced without a constriction narrow enough to create turbulence, and the shaping is done by
the position of the tongue body, the lips, and sometimes the velum. Because there is no contact point to
name, vowels are described in a continuous space rather than by discrete places, which makes them harder to
pin down and much more variable across dialects.

The primary dimensions are height, backness and rounding. Height is how close the tongue body comes to the
roof of the mouth, running from close or high vowels like the ee of see, through mid vowels like the e of
bed, to open or low vowels like the a of father. Backness is how far forward or back the tongue body sits,
from front vowels like ee and e, through central vowels like the schwa in the first syllable of about, to
back vowels like the oo of boot. Rounding is whether the lips are protruded. Most languages round their
back vowels and leave front vowels unrounded, but French, German, Turkish, Swedish and Mandarin all have
front rounded vowels, the sounds written u and eu in French, which are notoriously difficult for English
speakers precisely because English does not use that combination.

Acoustically these articulatory dimensions correspond closely to the first two resonant frequencies of the
vocal tract, called formants. The first formant, F1, varies inversely with height: high vowels have low F1,
around 300 hertz for a male speaker, while low vowels have high F1, around 700 to 800. The second formant,
F2, tracks backness, running from perhaps 2200 hertz for front vowels down to 900 for back ones. Plotting
F1 against F2 reproduces the traditional vowel quadrilateral almost exactly, which is a satisfying
convergence of two independent methods and one of the more robust results in the field.

Beyond quality, languages use several further vowel contrasts. Length distinguishes words in Finnish,
Japanese, Estonian and Classical Latin, where a long vowel is roughly twice the duration of a short one.
Nasalisation, produced by lowering the velum, is contrastive in French, Portuguese, Hindi and many West
African languages. Some languages use voice quality distinctions such as creaky or breathy phonation, as in
Gujarati and several Otomanguean languages of Mexico.

The typology of vowel systems shows a clear pattern of dispersion. Five-vowel systems of the type i, e, a,
o, u are by far the most common, found in Spanish, Japanese, Swahili and hundreds of others, and they
represent an efficient spreading of contrasts across the available acoustic space. Three-vowel systems
cluster at the corners, i, a, u. Systems with many vowels tend to add contrasts along new dimensions,
length, nasality or rounding, rather than cramming more qualities into the same space. This tendency was
formalised as the theory of adaptive dispersion, which predicts that inventories maximise perceptual
distinctiveness for a given size, and it fits the cross-linguistic data reasonably well without being
exceptionless.

sections.heading: The Syllable
sections.body:
Speakers of every language have strong intuitions about syllables. They can count them, they use them in
poetry and songwriting, they hyphenate by them, and children tapping out beats find them naturally. Yet
defining a syllable precisely has resisted a century of effort, and the phonetic correlates are surprisingly
elusive. Attempts to define it by chest pulses, by peaks of acoustic energy, or by jaw cycles all fail on
some cases. Most phonologists therefore treat the syllable as an abstract organisational unit whose
existence is justified by the patterns it explains rather than by any single physical measurement.

The standard internal structure is hierarchical. A syllable divides into an onset, the consonants before
the vowel, and a rhyme. The rhyme divides further into a nucleus, normally the vowel and the only obligatory
part, and a coda, the consonants after it. In the English word strength, str is the onset, e is the nucleus,
and ngth is the coda. The evidence for grouping nucleus and coda together as a rhyme, rather than grouping
onset and nucleus, is substantial: verse rhyme operates on exactly that constituent, syllable weight for
stress purposes is computed from it, and languages restrict its content in ways that ignore the onset.

Which segments can be a nucleus is determined by sonority, a scale of relative loudness or openness running
roughly from vowels at the top, through glides, liquids, nasals, then fricatives, and stops at the bottom.
The sonority sequencing principle states that sonority rises through the onset to a peak at the nucleus and
falls through the coda. This predicts that pla is a good syllable, since stop then liquid then vowel rises
correctly, while lpa is not. English mostly obeys it; the notorious exceptions all involve s, as in spring
and stop, where an s sits outside an otherwise well-formed onset. That behaviour has led many analysts to
treat such an s as attached higher in the structure rather than as a normal onset member, an admittedly
ad hoc but widely accepted solution.

In some languages, consonants themselves can be nuclei. The second syllable of English button and bottle
can be a syllabic n and a syllabic l with no vowel at all. Czech is famous for whole words without vowels,
such as the tongue-twister sentence about a wolf that has stuck a finger through a throat, where r and l
serve as nuclei.

Syllable weight is a further property with wide consequences. A syllable with a short vowel and no coda is
light; one with a long vowel, a diphthong, or a coda consonant is heavy. Many languages use weight to place
stress, to license tone, or to determine poetic metre. Classical Latin and Greek verse is built entirely on
weight rather than stress, which is why translating quantitative metre into English, a stress-timed
language, is fundamentally an approximation rather than a rendering.

sections.heading: Phonotactics: The Rules of Combination
sections.body:
Every language restricts which sounds may sit next to which, and where in a word each may appear. These
restrictions are its phonotactics, and speakers know them exhaustively without instruction. Presented with
the invented words blick, bnick and lbick, English speakers agree that the first is a fine potential word,
the second is odd but pronounceable, and the third is impossible. None exists in the vocabulary, so the
judgement cannot come from memory; it comes from a system.

English onsets illustrate the shape such systems take. A single consonant onset can be almost anything
except the ng of sing. Two-consonant onsets are heavily constrained: a stop may be followed by l or r,
giving pl, pr, bl, br, kl, kr, gl, gr, but not by a nasal, so bn and pm are excluded. The combination tl
and dl are excluded too, an interesting gap since tr and dr are fine, reflecting an articulatory difficulty
in moving from an alveolar stop to an alveolar lateral. Three-consonant onsets must begin with s, continue
with a voiceless stop, and end with a liquid or glide: spr, str, skr, spl, skw. That is the complete list,
and no English word violates it.

Other languages draw the lines elsewhere, and the differences are dramatic. Hawaiian permits only single
consonant onsets and no codas at all, so every syllable is a consonant plus a vowel or a bare vowel, which
is why English names entering Hawaiian acquire vowels between every consonant. Japanese permits codas only
for a nasal and the first half of a geminate, which is why the English word strike becomes sutoraiku with
vowels inserted to break up the impossible cluster. Georgian, at the other extreme, tolerates onsets of
six consonants. Nuxalk, of British Columbia, is reported to allow words with no vowels at all, though the
analysis of those forms remains debated.

Phonotactic knowledge shapes real behaviour beyond word judgements. It governs loanword adaptation, as the
Japanese example shows, and it explains characteristic second-language accents: a speaker whose language
bans codas will tend to add a vowel after English final consonants, and a speaker whose language bans
initial clusters will insert one before them. It also affects speech perception directly. Experiments have
shown that Japanese listeners report hearing a vowel that is not acoustically present when played a
consonant cluster their phonotactics forbid, a phenomenon called perceptual epenthesis. The grammar is not
merely a filter on production; it edits what people believe they heard.

There is also a gradient dimension that strict rules miss. Speakers rate some non-occurring sequences as
better than others, and those ratings track the statistical frequency of similar sequences in the
vocabulary. This has pushed many researchers toward probabilistic models of phonotactics rather than
categorical ones, and the debate between them is live.

sections.heading: Stress, Feet and Rhythm
sections.body:
Beyond the individual segment, languages organise speech into rhythmic patterns, and the most familiar of
these is stress: the relative prominence of one syllable over its neighbours. Stress is realised by a
combination of greater duration, higher pitch, greater intensity and, crucially in English, fuller vowel
quality, since unstressed English syllables tend to reduce toward the neutral vowel schwa.

Languages fall into broad classes by how stress is assigned. In fixed-stress languages, position is
predictable from the word edge: Finnish, Hungarian and Czech stress the first syllable, Polish and Swahili
the penultimate, French phrase-finally. In such languages stress carries no lexical information and is not
recorded in the dictionary. In free-stress or lexical-stress languages, position must be learned per word
and can distinguish meanings. English has minimal pairs of exactly this kind, where the noun and the verb
differ only in stress placement, as in a written permit versus to permit, an insult versus to insult, a
record versus to record. Russian and Spanish likewise use stress contrastively.

The theoretical account since the 1970s has been metrical phonology, developed by Mark Liberman, Alan
Prince, Bruce Hayes and others. It groups syllables into feet, small units each containing one strong
position. A trochaic foot is strong then weak, an iambic foot weak then strong. A language is then
characterised by which foot type it uses, whether feet are built from the left or right edge, and whether
foot construction is sensitive to syllable weight. English is broadly trochaic and weight-sensitive: heavy
syllables attract stress, which is why a word with a heavy penult tends to stress it. This machinery
explains not only main stress but secondary stress and the alternating strong-weak pattern that gives
English its characteristic beat, audible in a word like Mississippi.

Above the word, phrasal rhythm interacts with stress. English speakers adjust stress to avoid two strong
beats colliding, a process called the rhythm rule: the word thirteen is stressed on the second syllable in
isolation, but in the phrase thirteen men the stress shifts to the first to prevent adjacent prominences.
That shift is automatic and unconscious, and it is strong evidence that rhythm is computed at the phrase
level rather than looked up per word.

The older typology dividing languages into stress-timed, where stressed syllables recur at roughly equal
intervals, and syllable-timed, where syllables have roughly equal duration, is intuitively appealing and
was widely taught. Careful acoustic measurement has not supported the strict version: neither interval is
actually isochronous in the data. The perceptual difference between English and, say, Spanish is real, but
it appears to arise from differences in vowel reduction and syllable structure complexity rather than from
any timing mechanism, and the modern literature treats the labels as descriptive shorthand rather than as
a mechanism.

sections.heading: Tone and Pitch Accent
sections.body:
Roughly half the world's languages, including most of sub-Saharan Africa, much of East and Southeast Asia,
and large parts of Mesoamerica and New Guinea, use pitch to distinguish words. In such tone languages the
melody of a syllable is as much part of the word as its consonants and vowels, and getting it wrong
produces a different word, not merely an odd accent.

Mandarin Chinese is the standard textbook case, with four contrastive tones plus a neutral one. The
syllable pronounced ma means mother with a high level tone, hemp with a rising tone, horse with a falling
then rising tone, and scold with a sharply falling tone. These are not shades of emphasis; they are lexical
distinctions of exactly the same kind as the difference between pat and bat in English. Cantonese uses six
tones, Vietnamese six, Thai five.

Two broad types of tone system are usually distinguished. Register tone systems, common in Africa, use
level pitch targets, typically high and low, sometimes with a mid. Yoruba has three. Contour tone systems,
common in East Asia, use pitch movements as units in their own right. The distinction is not absolute, and
many systems mix both.

Tone participates in phonological processes just as segments do. Tone sandhi is the general name for
changes a tone undergoes next to another tone. Mandarin has a famous rule: a third tone followed by another
third tone becomes a second tone, so that the phrase meaning very good, which would be two third tones, is
pronounced with a rising tone on the first syllable. Speakers are unaware of applying this. In many African
languages tones spread across whole phrases, float free of the syllable that carried them when that
syllable is deleted, and dock onto neighbours. Such behaviour was the original motivation for
