autosegmental phonology, proposed by John Goldsmith in 1976, which represents tones on a separate tier from
segments, linked by association lines. That representational move solved a class of problems that had
resisted linear rules and became one of the field's durable innovations.

Between full tone languages and stress languages lies pitch accent, where pitch is contrastive but only one
syllable per word carries a specification, the rest being predictable. Japanese is the usual example: words
are distinguished by where the pitch drops, so that the sequence hashi with an early drop, a late drop, or
no drop corresponds to chopsticks, bridge and edge respectively in the Tokyo variety. Swedish and Norwegian
have a two-way tonal contrast on the stressed syllable, and Serbo-Croatian and Ancient Greek had comparable
systems. Whether pitch accent constitutes a genuine third type or simply a small tone system is genuinely
contested; several prominent researchers argue the category should be abandoned, and the question is not
settled.

sections.heading: Intonation and Prosody Above the Word
sections.body:
Even languages that do not use pitch to distinguish words use it constantly to structure utterances and
convey attitude. This is intonation, and it operates over phrases and whole sentences rather than over
syllables. It is the layer of speech that carries whether you are asking or telling, which piece of
information is new, where one idea ends and the next begins, and a great deal of emotional and social
meaning that no transcription of words captures.

The dominant analytic framework, developed by Janet Pierrehumbert in her 1980 dissertation and elaborated
into the system known as ToBI, treats an intonation contour not as a continuous curve but as a sequence of
discrete tonal targets, high and low, associated either with stressed syllables, where they are called pitch
accents, or with the edges of phrases, where they are called boundary tones. The audible melody is then
produced by interpolation between targets. This decomposition explains why the same contour can stretch
over one word or twenty: the targets stay the same and the interpolation adjusts.

Several functions are worth separating. Focus marking uses pitch prominence to signal what is
informationally important, and in English it can move freely: the sentence about someone not stealing a book
means something different depending on which word is accented, contrasting the person, the action or the
object. Many languages cannot do this and instead reorder words or use particles to mark focus, which is why
translating English focus into them requires syntactic rather than prosodic changes. Phrasing marks where
constituents begin and end and can disambiguate sentences that are structurally identical in writing;
speakers reliably signal, with pitch and duration, whether an adjective applies to one noun or two.
Sentence type is often signalled tonally, with a rising boundary tone common on questions across many
languages, though this is a tendency rather than a universal.

Final lengthening and pauses accompany intonational boundaries. Syllables at the end of a phrase are
measurably longer, often by thirty to fifty percent, than the same syllables medially, and this duration
cue is used by listeners and by infants learning to segment speech.

Two cautions matter here. First, intonational meaning is more variable across languages and dialects than
people assume, and confident claims that a rising terminal signals uncertainty are culturally parochial;
several varieties of English use rises on ordinary statements as a matter of dialect. Second, the
interpretation of intonation is bound up with attitude, personality and social identity in ways that resist
clean formalisation. This is one of the areas where phonology grades into pragmatics and sociolinguistics
and where honest description outruns theory. The formal apparatus captures the shapes well; what the shapes
mean is a much less settled matter.

sections.heading: Phonological Processes
sections.body:
When phonemes are strung together, they change. These systematic changes are phonological processes, and a
handful of types account for the overwhelming majority of what languages do. Learning the catalogue makes
otherwise bewildering data patterns fall into place quickly.

Assimilation, the most common process by far, makes one sound more like a neighbour. English prefixes
illustrate it clearly: the negative prefix appears as in before most stems, but as im before labials, as in
impossible and improbable, and as ing before velars in the pronunciation of incomplete, where the nasal
takes on the place of the following consonant. Assimilation may be anticipatory, where a sound changes to
match what follows, or perseverative, where it matches what precedes. It may be partial, copying only one
feature, or total, making the two segments identical.

Dissimilation makes two similar sounds less alike, and it is much rarer. Latin words with two r sounds
sometimes changed one to l, which is why the suffix in military is lar rather than rar after a stem
containing r. Grassmann's Law in Ancient Greek and Sanskrit, formulated in 1863, deaspirated the first of
two aspirates in a root, and it is the classic textbook case.

Deletion removes a segment. English speakers routinely delete the middle consonant in clusters, so that
friendship is often pronounced without the d and the word months loses its th. Vowel deletion, or syncope,
turns family into a two-syllable word in casual speech. Insertion, or epenthesis, adds one, typically to
repair a structure the language does not tolerate: many English speakers insert a p between the m and th of
warmth, and Spanish speakers historically added an e before initial s clusters, which is why Latin schola
became Spanish escuela.

Lenition weakens a consonant, typically making it more sonorous and shorter, and it very often applies
between vowels. American English flapping is a familiar case: the t and d of writer and rider both become a
quick tap between a stressed and unstressed vowel, which is why the two words differ, for many speakers,
only in the length of the preceding vowel. Spanish intervocalic b, d and g are pronounced as fricatives
rather than stops by the same logic. Fortition, the opposite, strengthens, and typically occurs at the
beginnings of words or stressed syllables.

Neutralisation eliminates a contrast in some position. German, Dutch, Russian and Polish all devoice
obstruents at the end of a word, so that the German words for advice and wheel are pronounced identically
although they are spelled differently and behave differently when a suffix follows. Metathesis swaps the
order of segments, as in the historical development of English bird from an earlier form with the r after
the vowel. Compensatory lengthening lengthens a vowel when a following consonant is lost, which explains
many long vowels in the history of English and Greek.

sections.heading: Rules and Constraints: Two Ways to Model a System
sections.body:
Once the processes are catalogued, the theoretical question is how to represent the knowledge that produces
them. Two answers have dominated the last sixty years, and understanding the difference between them is
understanding modern phonology's central argument.

The rule-based approach, established by Chomsky and Halle's The Sound Pattern of English in 1968, posits an
underlying representation stored in the lexicon and an ordered series of rewrite rules that transform it
into the surface form. A rule has the shape: some feature changes to some value, in some environment. The
English plural is derived by taking a single underlying form and applying a voicing assimilation rule, plus
an epenthesis rule that inserts a vowel after sibilants to give the extra syllable in horses and buses.
Crucially the rules are ordered, and the ordering does explanatory work. If epenthesis applies before
voicing assimilation, the inserted vowel means the ending follows a vowel and correctly surfaces as voiced;
the opposite order gives the wrong result. Whole analyses turn on such interactions, and the phenomena of
feeding, where one rule creates the input for another, and bleeding, where one destroys it, became a rich
source of evidence about mental organisation.

The constraint-based approach, Optimality Theory, was introduced by Alan Prince and Paul Smolensky in 1993
and rapidly reoriented the field. It abandons ordered derivations. Instead a generator proposes an
unlimited set of candidate outputs for any input, and a ranked set of violable constraints evaluates them;
the winner is the candidate that best satisfies the highest-ranked constraints. Constraints come in two
families: markedness constraints penalise structures that are difficult or rare, such as codas or voiced
final obstruents, and faithfulness constraints penalise any difference between input and output. A language
is then nothing but a particular ranking of a universal constraint set, and typology becomes the study of
possible rankings, a claim called factorial typology.

The appeal of Optimality Theory is that it explains conspiracies, cases where several unrelated-looking
rules all act to enforce a single surface pattern. In a rule system that coincidence is unexplained; under
ranked constraints it falls out automatically, because one high-ranked constraint drives all of them. The
costs are real too. Opacity, where a surface form shows the effect of a rule whose triggering environment
is no longer visible, is straightforward under ordered rules and genuinely difficult under classical
Optimality Theory, prompting a proliferation of repairs including sympathy theory, stratal versions and
candidate chains.

Neither framework has decisively won, and a good analyst can usually state the same generalisation in
either. Recent work has moved toward probabilistic and learning-based models, including maximum entropy
grammars that assign weights rather than strict rankings, and exemplar models that dispense with abstract
underlying forms altogether. Which of these is closest to what a speaker actually does remains open.

sections.heading: Morphophonology: Where Sound Meets Structure
sections.body:
Phonology does not operate on a uniform stream. Words have internal structure, and the boundaries between
meaningful pieces, morphemes, condition what sounds do. The study of that interaction is morphophonology,
and it is where phonological analysis most often earns its keep, because it explains alternations that look
irregular but are not.

The English plural is the standard first example, and it is worth working through completely. The ending
has three pronunciations: an s sound after cats, maps and cliffs, a z sound after dogs, cans and trees, and
an extra syllable in horses, buses, churches and judges. The traditional analysis posits a single stored
form, a z, and two rules. First, if the stem ends in a sibilant, one of the s-like or sh-like sounds,
insert a vowel to break up the sequence, because English does not tolerate two adjacent sibilants in that
position. Second, if no vowel was inserted, make the ending agree in voicing with the preceding sound. Three
surface forms, one stored item, two general rules that also derive the past tense ending and the possessive.
That economy is the argument for the analysis.

Alternations can be far less transparent. English has a systematic pattern where a vowel shortens before
certain suffixes: divine but divinity, serene but serenity, sane but sanity, profound but profundity. This
trisyllabic laxing was a centrepiece of The Sound Pattern of English, treated as a live rule of the modern
language derived from underlying long vowels. Subsequent work has questioned that: the pattern has many
exceptions, obesity keeps its long vowel, and speakers do not reliably extend it to new words. The current
consensus leans toward treating such alternations as partly memorised and only partly productive, which is
a significant retreat from the strong generative position and an honest one.

Boundaries also block processes. English flapping applies inside a word and across some word boundaries but
is sensitive to structure. German final devoicing applies at the end of a word or a stem but not before a
vowel-initial suffix, which is why the noun for wheel devoices in isolation but not in its plural. The
existence of such effects motivated lexical phonology, developed by Paul Kiparsky and Kaisa Mohanan in the
early 1980s, which organises the grammar into strata: some rules apply early, alongside word formation,
and may have exceptions and change the stress pattern, while others apply late, across the board and
without exception.

Reduplication, where a copy of part of a word marks a grammatical function, is a further morphophonological
domain of considerable interest, since it requires the grammar to copy phonological material rather than
simply insert a fixed string. It is common in Austronesian and in many languages of the Americas, and
whether it belongs to morphology or phonology is precisely the kind of boundary dispute this subfield lives on.

sections.heading: Acquisition, Variation and Sound Change
sections.body:
A phonological system is not a static object. It is learned in infancy, it varies systematically across a
speech community, and it drifts across generations. These three facts are connected, and together they
explain where sound systems come from.

Acquisition begins before birth: newborns show preference for the rhythmic pattern of the language heard in
utero. Through the first year infants perform a striking reorganisation. At six months they discriminate
essentially any phonetic contrast presented to them, including ones absent from the surrounding language.
By ten to twelve months that ability has narrowed to native contrasts, a process Janet Werker and Richard
Tees documented in influential work published in 1984. Production lags perception by a wide margin.
Children who cannot yet produce a contrast can nonetheless hear it, which is why a child who says wabbit
will reject an adult who imitates them. Typical order of mastery runs from stops and nasals early to
fricatives, affricates and liquids later, with r and the th sounds among the last in English, often not
fully controlled until age six or seven.

Variation across a community is not noise but structure. William Labov's studies from the 1960s onward
showed that phonological variables correlate systematically with social class, age, gender, ethnicity and
speech style, and that speakers shift within their own range depending on context. His work on the
pronunciation of r in New York City department stores demonstrated that a single variable could be
predicted from the social position of the speaker and the formality of the moment. Variation of this kind
is the raw material of change: a variant that is favoured by one group spreads, and if it eventually becomes
categorical, the system has changed.

Sound change itself has recognisable mechanisms. The most important is phonologisation, in which an
automatic phonetic effect becomes a contrast in its own right. Vowels are naturally longer before voiced
consonants everywhere; in English that predictable difference has grown large enough that many speakers now
carry the contrast on vowel length rather than on the consonant, which for flapping dialects is the only
thing distinguishing writer from rider. Nasal vowels in French arose the same way, from vowels nasalised
before a nasal consonant that later disappeared.

Change is often regular, a finding formalised by the Neogrammarians in the 1870s, whose slogan held that
sound laws admit no exceptions. Grimm's Law, describing the systematic consonant shifts from
Proto-Indo-European to Germanic, and Verner's Law, which in 1875 explained Grimm's apparent exceptions by
reference to the position of the original accent, remain the showcase demonstrations. Yet lexical
diffusion, in which a change spreads word by word rather than all at once, is also well documented, and the
tension between the two accounts is unresolved and probably reflects genuinely different kinds of change.

sections.heading: Doing an Analysis: Procedure, Pitfalls and Open Questions
sections.body:
Faced with a page of transcribed data from an unfamiliar language, a phonologist follows a fairly stable
procedure, and the discipline it imposes is what prevents the commonest errors.

Those errors are worth naming. The first is trusting orthography: spelling reflects history, not
pronunciation. The second is assuming your own categories are universal, so that an English speaker fails to
record a length or tone distinction because English lacks it. The third is insufficient data: a gap in a
small corpus may be accidental, and claiming a rule from four examples is unsafe. The fourth is ignoring
morphology, which produces phantom rules when an alternation is really about which suffix was attached.

Genuine open questions remain at the centre of the field. How abstract are underlying representations, and
do speakers store abstract forms at all or memorise variants and generalise over them? Are distinctive
features innate, or learned from the phonetics of the ambient language? Does the syllable have any
consistent phonetic definition? None has a settled answer, and a source presenting one confidently is
reporting a school of thought rather than a result.
steps: Transcribe the data phonetically, in narrow transcription, recording every audible detail including aspiration, length, nasalisation and tone, even where you suspect it is irrelevant. Detail can be discarded later; it cannot be recovered.
Build an inventory of every distinct sound observed, noting for each the environments it appears in: word-initially, between vowels, before a consonant, word-finally, stressed or unstressed.
Search for minimal pairs. Any pair of words differing in meaning and in exactly one sound in the same position establishes those two sounds as separate phonemes immediately.

For sounds with no minimal pair, compare their environment lists. Overlapping lists mean the sounds may still contrast or be in free variation; complementary lists, with no shared environment, mean they are allophones of one phoneme.

Decide which allophone is basic. Take the one with the wider, less specifiable distribution as underlying and derive the restricted one by rule, since stating the special case is simpler than stating the general one.
State the rule in features, not lists of segments. A rule that must enumerate six sounds has probably missed the natural class uniting them, and the enumeration signals an incorrect analysis.

Check the rule against every form in the data, including those you did not use to formulate it. One genuine counterexample refutes it; look for an overlooked conditioning factor before adding an exception.
Examine syllable structure and phonotactics separately: list attested onsets, nuclei and codas, and note which logically possible combinations never occur.
Look for morpheme boundaries before concluding that an alternation is purely phonological. Compare related word forms to see whether the change tracks a suffix rather than a sound.
Test productivity where you can, by asking a speaker to inflect an invented word. A rule speakers extend to novel forms is live; one they do not is probably memorised.
Write the analysis so that another person can derive every surface form from your underlying forms and rules, and state explicitly which forms you cannot account for.

guides.title: Prosody, Stress & Intonation
guides.summary: A comprehensive account of the melody, rhythm and prominence of speech: the acoustic ingredients of prosody, how word stress and pitch accent work, the prosodic hierarchy, rhythm typology, intonational systems and their meanings, and how prosody is acquired, measured, disordered and learned in a second language.

sections.heading: What Prosody Is and Why It Carries So Much of the Message
sections.body:
Prosody is everything in speech that rides on top of the individual consonants and vowels: which syllables are made prominent, how the voice rises and falls, where the speaker breaks the stream into chunks, how fast the chunks go, and how loud, breathy, creaky or tense the voice sounds while producing them. Linguists sometimes call these features suprasegmental, meaning they are laid over the segments rather than being segments themselves. A single syllable such as the English word "right" has a fixed segmental identity, but it can be said as a flat acknowledgement, a rising question, a sceptical drawl, an angry bark or a delighted exclamation, and listeners reliably tell those apart. The segments did not change. Everything that changed was prosodic.

The reason prosody matters is that it is not decoration. It carries at least four distinct kinds of information simultaneously, and the listener unpacks all four in real time. First, lexical information: in many languages, including English, Spanish, Russian and Greek, the position of stress can distinguish one word from another, so that English "INsight" and "inCITE" or Spanish "hablo" (I speak) and "habló" (he spoke) differ only in where prominence falls. Second, grammatical information: prosody tells you where phrases begin and end, which resolves structural ambiguities that the words alone leave open. Third, informational structure: prosody marks which part of an utterance is new, contrastive or the point of the sentence, and which part is background already shared with the listener. Fourth, interpersonal and affective information: attitude, politeness, sarcasm, uncertainty, dominance, regional identity and emotional state all leak into the melody and the voice quality.

There is a fifth function that is easy to overlook because it is so pervasive. Prosody is the primary device by which speech is made processable at all. Continuous speech contains almost none of the tidy white space that separates written words. Listeners segment the stream using rhythmic and melodic regularities, and infants exploit exactly these cues to break into a language they cannot yet understand. Strip the prosody out of a recording, as early speech synthesisers effectively did, and intelligibility collapses long before the segments become unrecognisable, because the listener no longer knows where to look for structure.

A useful working distinction runs between linguistic prosody, which is conventionalised, language-specific and part of the grammar, and paralinguistic prosody, which is gradient, largely cross-culturally shared and expressive. A rising terminal on an English yes-no question is grammatical. Speaking faster and higher when excited is paralinguistic. The boundary is genuinely fuzzy — some phenomena, such as the association of high pitch with politeness or deference, sit ambiguously between the two, and researchers still disagree about where particular effects belong.

sections.heading: The Acoustic Ingredients: Pitch, Loudness, Duration and Voice Quality
sections.body:
Prosody is perceived through four principal acoustic dimensions, each with a physical measure and a perceptual counterpart that only imperfectly tracks it. Getting this correspondence right matters, because almost all confusion in this field comes from conflating the physical signal with the impression it makes.

The first is fundamental frequency, written F0, the rate at which the vocal folds open and close during voiced sound. It is measured in hertz, cycles per second. Typical modal speaking F0 runs roughly 100 to 130 Hz for adult male voices, 180 to 230 Hz for adult female voices and 250 to 400 Hz for young children, with wide individual variation and enormous within-utterance range. The perceptual correlate is pitch, and the mapping is nonlinear: equal ratios, not equal differences, sound like equal intervals. A rise from 100 to 200 Hz and a rise from 200 to 400 Hz are both one octave and sound comparably large, which is why researchers usually convert to semitones, where one semitone is a frequency ratio of the twelfth root of two, about 1.0595, or to the ERB or Bark scales derived from auditory filtering.

The second is intensity, the acoustic power in the signal, measured in decibels on a logarithmic scale where a 10 dB increase corresponds to roughly a doubling of perceived loudness. Conversational speech at one metre typically sits around 60 dB SPL. Intensity is a weaker cue to prominence than intuition suggests; speakers do push harder on stressed syllables, but listeners weight pitch and duration far more heavily, and intensity varies with microphone distance and vowel identity in ways that swamp the linguistic signal.

The third is duration, measured in milliseconds. Segment durations in running speech range from perhaps 30 ms for a flap to 300 ms or more for a stressed diphthong before a pause. Duration is a robust and heavily used prosodic cue: stressed syllables are longer, syllables before a phrase boundary are lengthened by 20 to 100 per cent in a phenomenon called pre-boundary or final lengthening, and speech rate itself, usually reported in syllables per second, typically 4 to 7 for relaxed conversation, is an independent prosodic variable.

The fourth is voice quality, sometimes called phonation type, which describes how the vocal folds vibrate rather than how fast. Modal voice is the ordinary setting. Breathy voice leaves a glottal gap so that turbulent noise mixes with periodicity. Creaky voice, also called vocal fry or laryngealisation, involves irregular low-frequency pulses, often below 70 Hz, and in English it clusters at the ends of phrases and has become a salient sociolinguistic variable. Tense or pressed voice raises the ratio of high-frequency energy. Voice quality carries phrase-boundary information, affect and, in some languages, lexical contrasts.

sections.heading: Syllables, Weight and the Units That Prosody Operates On
sections.body:
Prosody does not attach to segments one at a time. It attaches to syllables, and above them to larger constituents. Understanding the syllable is therefore prerequisite to understanding stress at all, and it turns out to be one of the more slippery objects in linguistics: speakers have strong intuitions about how many syllables a word has, yet a fully general phonetic definition has never been agreed.

The standard structural model divides the syllable into an onset and a rhyme, with the rhyme subdividing into a nucleus and a coda. In the English word "strand", the onset is the cluster /str/, the nucleus is the vowel /æ/ and the coda is /nd/. The nucleus is obligatory and is normally a vowel, though some languages allow syllabic consonants, as in the second syllable of English "button" or the Czech word "vlk" (wolf), which has no vowel at all. Onsets and codas are optional and their permitted shapes are tightly language-specific: Japanese and Hawaiian permit essentially no consonant clusters, Georgian and Polish permit extraordinary ones.

The critical prosodic property is syllable weight. In a great many languages a syllable counts as heavy if its rhyme contains either a long vowel or diphthong, or a short vowel followed by at least one consonant, and light otherwise. A common formalisation uses the mora, a unit of weight: a short vowel contributes one mora, a long vowel two, and a coda consonant one in languages where codas count. So Latin "pa" is monomoraic and light, while "pā" and "pat" are bimoraic and heavy. Some languages, notably Japanese, treat the mora as the primary rhythmic unit outright; Japanese speakers count "Nippon" as four beats, ni-p-po-n, not two syllables.

Weight matters because stress systems in dozens of unrelated languages are weight-sensitive: they place stress on heavy syllables in preference to light ones. Classical Latin is the textbook case. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable if that syllable is heavy, and otherwise retracts to the antepenultimate. So "amīcus" stresses the heavy penult, while "fēmina" retracts because the penult is light. Arabic, Hindi, Yup'ik and many Australian languages show weight-sensitive systems of comparable regularity.

Above the syllable sits the foot, a grouping of usually two syllables (occasionally three) with one designated strong. A trochee is strong-weak, an iamb weak-strong. Whether a language builds trochees or iambs, whether it builds them from the left or the right edge of the word, and whether it tolerates leftover unfooted syllables, together account for a large share of the world's stress patterns in the metrical theory developed by Mark Liberman and Alan Prince in 1977 and elaborated by Bruce Hayes through the 1980s and 1990s. The Iambic-Trochaic Law, a perceptual generalisation, holds that elements contrasting in duration group naturally with the long element final, while elements contrasting in intensity group with the loud element initial.

sections.heading: Word Stress: What Makes a Syllable Prominent
sections.body:
Word stress is the property whereby one syllable of a polysyllabic word is more prominent than the others. The prominence is abstract: it is a structural fact about the word stored in the mental lexicon, and it is realised phonetically in different ways depending on the language and on where the word sits in the sentence. The commonest mistake is to equate stress with loudness. Loudness contributes, but the dominant physical exponents of English stress are, in rough order of importance, pitch movement, duration and vowel quality, with intensity trailing.

Vowel quality deserves particular emphasis because in English it is nearly decisive. English unstressed syllables systematically reduce their vowel toward schwa, the mid-central vowel written as an upside-down e, or toward a reduced high vowel. Compare "photograph", "photography" and "photographic": the same root supplies three different stress placements, and every time stress moves, the vowels that lose it collapse to schwa while the vowel that gains it takes its full value. This coupling of stress and vowel reduction is characteristic of English, Dutch, German and Russian but is absent in Spanish, Italian, Japanese and most of the world's languages, where unstressed vowels keep their quality.

A crucial distinction separates lexical stress from sentence-level accent. Lexical stress specifies which syllable of a word is eligible for prominence; it is stored with the word. Whether that syllable actually receives a pitch movement in a given utterance depends on the sentence: in "I bought a BANANA", the second syllable of banana receives a full pitch accent, but in "I bought a banana MILKSHAKE" the word banana is deaccented and its stressed syllable is merely relatively longer than its neighbours, with no pitch excursion at all. Researchers therefore distinguish stress, a lexical property, from accent, its realisation in a given utterance, and from prominence, the perceptual outcome.

English also distinguishes degrees. Traditional descriptions recognise primary stress, secondary stress and unstressed, so that "constitution" has primary stress on the third syllable and secondary on the first. Secondary stress is real — the first vowel resists reduction and carries some duration — but it does not attract pitch accents in the way primary stress does.

Compound stress rules add another layer. English generally stresses the left member of a compound noun and the right member of a corresponding phrase, giving the classic minimal pairs "a BLACKbird" (a species) versus "a black BIRD" (any dark bird), or "the WHITE House" versus "a white HOUSE". Speakers apply this rule productively to novel compounds, which shows it is a live generalisation rather than a set of memorised exceptions. There are genuine irregularities — "apple PIE" takes phrasal stress despite being a compound — and the boundaries of the rule remain a live research question rather than a settled matter.

sections.heading: Stress Systems Across the World's Languages
sections.body:
Comparative work, most systematically in the World Atlas of Language Structures survey of several hundred languages, shows that stress systems fall into a small number of recurring types, and that the type is largely predictable from a handful of parameters.

The first type is fixed stress: stress lands on a syllable identified purely by counting from a word edge, regardless of the word's internal makeup. Finnish, Hungarian, Czech and Icelandic put stress on the first syllable of every word without exception, which is why Czech sounds so relentlessly front-loaded to outsiders. Polish and Swahili put it on the penultimate. Classical Mongolian and French are usually described as final, though French is better analysed as having phrase-final rather than word-final prominence, since an isolated French word carries prominence on its last full syllable but within a phrase only the last word does. Fixed-stress systems carry no lexical contrast — stress can never distinguish two words — so they instead serve as a reliable word-boundary cue, which listeners demonstrably exploit.

The second type is weight-sensitive stress, where position depends on the heaviness of candidate syllables. Latin, as noted, and Classical Arabic are canonical. In Cairene Arabic, stress falls on a final superheavy syllable, otherwise on a heavy penult, otherwise it is computed by counting moras from the left. These systems are algorithmic: given the segmental shape of a word, the stress position is derivable, so it need not be memorised.

The third type is lexical or free stress, where the position must be learned word by word because it is not predictable from shape or position. Russian is the classic case, with stress that can fall on any syllable and that shifts across the inflectional paradigm of a single noun, so that Russian dictionaries mark it and Russian children take years to master it. English, Spanish, Greek, Italian and Portuguese all have lexical stress with strong statistical tendencies but genuine unpredictability at the margins. English words of Germanic origin overwhelmingly stress the first syllable of the root, while Romance and Latinate borrowings brought a competing system, and the coexistence of the two is responsible for much of the apparent chaos.

A fourth possibility is no word stress at all. Several languages, including many varieties of Korean, Bengali and some West African languages, have been argued to lack a word-level prominence system entirely, using phrasal tonal patterns instead. Claims of this kind are contested, because absence of stress is hard to prove and easy to mistake for a system that is simply realised differently from the European template. This is a genuine area of unresolved disagreement rather than settled fact, and the descriptive literature should be read with that in mind.

sections.heading: Tone and Pitch Accent: When Melody Is Lexical
sections.body:
In roughly 40 to 50 per cent of the world's languages, pitch is not merely an intonational overlay; it is part of the identity of the word, exactly as consonants and vowels are. These are tone languages, and they are the majority pattern in sub-Saharan Africa, East and Southeast Asia and Mesoamerica.

A tone language assigns a pitch specification to syllables or morphemes lexically. Mandarin Chinese is the most familiar example, with four contrastive tones plus a neutral tone: the syllable "ma" means mother with a high level tone, hemp with a rising tone, horse with a falling-rising tone and scold with a sharply falling tone. Cantonese has six contrastive tones, Thai five, Vietnamese six with additional voice-quality distinctions. African tone systems often use fewer levels — two, high and low, is very common — but combine them into rich morphological systems, so that in many Bantu languages the difference between a past and a present tense, or between a relative and a main clause, is carried entirely by tone.

Tone languages divide broadly into register systems, which contrast static pitch levels, and contour systems, which contrast pitch movements. Most Asian systems are contour-heavy; most African systems are register-based, with contours arising from the association of two level tones to a single syllable. Autosegmental phonology, developed by John Goldsmith in his 1976 dissertation, models tones as a separate tier of representation linked by association lines to the segmental tier. This elegantly explains phenomena that defeat a linear model: tone stability, where a tone survives the deletion of its vowel and relinks elsewhere; tone spreading, where a high tone extends rightward across following syllables; and downstep, where a high tone is realised lower than a preceding high because a floating low tone intervenes.

Pitch accent languages sit between tone and stress. In these systems only one syllable per word, at most, bears a tonal specification, and many words bear none. Tokyo Japanese is the standard example: "hashi" with an accent on the first mora means chopsticks, with an accent on the second means bridge, and with no accent at all means edge, a distinction audible only when a following particle reveals whether the pitch drops. Swedish and Norwegian contrast two accents, traditionally called acute and grave, so that Swedish "anden" means the duck with one and the spirit with the other. Serbo-Croatian and Ancient Greek had comparable systems.

Whether pitch accent is a genuine third category or simply a subtype of one of the other two is genuinely disputed. Larry Hyman has argued forcefully that there is no coherent pitch-accent prototype, and that such languages are best described as having a restricted tone system, a stress system with tonal exponents, or a hybrid. The label remains widely used as a convenient description even by researchers who doubt its theoretical status.

sections.heading: The Prosodic Hierarchy: How Speech Is Chunked
sections.body:
Speech is not a flat sequence of syllables. It is organised into a nested hierarchy of domains, each with its own characteristic phonetic signature and each serving as the domain within which particular phonological rules apply. The standard hierarchy, developed principally by Elisabeth Selkirk, Marina Nespor and Irene Vogel in the 1980s, runs from the smallest unit upward: the mora, the syllable, the foot, the prosodic word, the phonological phrase, the intonational phrase and the utterance.

Each level is diagnosed by evidence rather than assumed. The prosodic word is the domain of word stress and of many segmental rules; in English it is the domain within which aspiration of voiceless stops applies at the beginning of a stressed syllable. The phonological phrase corresponds roughly to a syntactic phrase and is the domain of rhythmic adjustments. The intonational phrase is the largest unit routinely relevant to intonation, and it is the one with the most audible boundary signature: pre-boundary lengthening of the final syllable, a boundary tone, an optional pause and a pitch reset at the start of the next phrase. Fluent speakers produce intonational phrases of roughly 1 to 3 seconds containing 5 to 15 syllables, though this varies with style and speech rate.

Two structural principles govern the hierarchy in its classical form. Strict Layering requires each unit to be composed exhaustively of units of exactly the next level down, with no skipping and no recursion. The Strict Layer Hypothesis has since been substantially weakened; considerable evidence supports recursion, particularly in prosodic words containing clitics and in nested phonological phrases, and most contemporary work in Optimality Theory treats layering as a set of violable constraints rather than an inviolable law.

The practical consequence of hierarchy is that boundary strength is graded. A word boundary, a phrase boundary and a sentence boundary are not equivalent; they are marked by progressively greater lengthening, larger pitch resets and longer pauses. Perceptual studies show listeners are exquisitely sensitive to this gradation, and can identify boundary strength reliably from lengthening alone with the pitch removed.

Where prosodic boundaries fall is influenced by syntax but not determined by it. A long subject noun phrase will typically be phrased separately from its predicate; a short one will not. Speech rate compresses phrasing, so the same sentence read slowly may contain four intonational phrases and read quickly only one. Breathing exerts an independent pressure, since inhalation must occur somewhere and speakers place it at prosodic boundaries where possible. The relationship between syntactic structure and prosodic structure is therefore one of systematic but imperfect correspondence, a fact that has generated a large theoretical literature under the heading of the syntax-phonology interface.

sections.heading: Rhythm: Stress-Timing, Syllable-Timing and What Measurement Shows
sections.body:
The intuition that different languages have characteristically different rhythms is old and robust. English and Arabic sound to speakers of Spanish or Italian like a series of heavy beats with compressed material between them; Spanish and Italian sound to English speakers like a rapid even patter, sometimes described unkindly as machine-gun-like. Kenneth Pike in 1945 and David Abercrombie in 1967 formalised this as a typology: stress-timed languages were said to have roughly equal intervals between stressed syllables, with unstressed syllables compressed to fit, while syllable-timed languages were said to have roughly equal syllable durations. A third class, mora-timed, was proposed for Japanese, where the mora rather than the syllable was said to be the isochronous unit.

The typology was intuitively compelling and, in its strong form, turned out to be false. When researchers actually measured inter-stress intervals in English, they found no isochrony whatsoever. The interval between stresses grows steadily with the number of intervening syllables; there is some compression, but it recovers only a small fraction of the added duration. The same negative result emerged for syllable duration in Spanish and for mora duration in Japanese. By the 1980s the strong isochrony hypothesis was widely regarded as empirically dead.

What survived, and what the field has spent thirty years reconstructing, is that the perceptual difference is real even though the timing claim was wrong. The modern explanation locates rhythm not in isochrony but in the consequences of two independent properties: syllable structure complexity and vowel reduction. Languages permitting complex consonant clusters have highly variable syllable durations; languages that reduce unstressed vowels to schwa further increase the contrast between strong and weak syllables. Franck Ramus, Marina Nespor and Jacques Mehler proposed in 1999 a set of measurable rhythm metrics: %V, the proportion of the utterance occupied by vocalic intervals, and ΔC, the standard deviation of consonantal interval durations. Plotted against each other, these separate English, Dutch and Polish (low %V, high ΔC) from Spanish, Italian and Catalan (high %V, low ΔC), with Japanese in a corner of its own. Later refinements, the Pairwise Variability Index of Esther Grabe and Ee Ling Low and the normalised nPVI, measure successive-interval contrast and normalise for speech rate.

These metrics work, but they are noisier than early enthusiasm suggested. They are sensitive to speech rate, to the particular text read, to the speaker and to segmentation decisions, and different studies using different metrics have sometimes placed the same language in different regions. The honest summary is that rhythm class is a useful gradient description, not a discrete typology, and that languages populate a continuum rather than three boxes. Newborn infants can nonetheless discriminate languages from different rhythm classes on low-pass-filtered speech and cannot discriminate within a class, which is strong evidence that whatever the metrics are imperfectly capturing is psychologically real.

sections.heading: Intonation and the Autosegmental-Metrical Model
sections.body:
Intonation is the use of pitch at the phrase level for meanings that are not lexical. Two broad traditions have described it. The older British school, running from Harold Palmer through J. D. O'Connor and Gordon Arnold to David Crystal, described intonation in terms of tunes: a phrase was divided into a prehead, head, nucleus and tail, with the nucleus being the last accented syllable and the tune being characterised by whether it fell, rose, fell-rose, rose-fell or stayed level. This tradition is descriptively rich and remains the basis of much British English language teaching.

The dominant contemporary framework is the autosegmental-metrical model, usually abbreviated AM, which emerged from Janet Pierrehumbert's 1980 MIT dissertation and was consolidated in work with Mary Beckman and others. Its central claim is that an intonation contour is not a holistic shape but a sequence of discrete tonal targets, drawn from a small inventory, with the pitch between targets produced by simple interpolation. Only two primitive tones are needed, H (high) and L (low), and everything else is built from them.

Tones come in two structural kinds. Pitch accents associate with metrically strong syllables and are marked with an asterisk indicating which tone aligns with the stressed syllable. English is usually analysed as having six: H*, a simple high accent, the default declarative accent; L*, a low accent; L+H*, a rise onto the accented syllable, associated with contrastive focus; L*+H, a low accented syllable followed by a rise, associated with uncertainty or incredulity; H+!H*, a downstepped accent; and H*+L in some inventories. Edge tones mark boundaries: phrase accents, written H- or L-, mark the end of an intermediate phrase, and boundary tones, written H% or L%, mark the end of a full intonational phrase.

The model's power is combinatorial. The falling declarative of English is H* L-L%. The canonical yes-no question rise is L* H-H%. The so-called continuation rise, signalling more to come, is often H* H-L% or L* L-H%. The distinctive "uptalk" or high rising terminal on statements uses a rise where a fall would be expected. The plateau contour L* H-L% carries a characteristic flavour of the obvious or the resigned.

Out of this grew ToBI, Tones and Break Indices, a transcription standard first agreed at conferences in 1991 and 1992 and now the lingua franca of intonation research. A ToBI transcription has a tone tier carrying the AM labels, a break index tier scoring each word boundary from 0 (clitic-like fusion) to 4 (full intonational phrase boundary), an orthographic tier and a miscellaneous tier. Language-specific ToBI systems now exist for German, Japanese, Korean, Greek, Spanish and many others, though the tone inventories differ and cross-language comparison of ToBI labels must be done carefully.

sections.heading: Focus, Givenness and the Information Structure of Utterances
sections.body:
Perhaps the most important grammatical work prosody does in English is marking information structure: which part of an utterance is new or contrastive, and which is presupposed. This system is largely invisible in writing, which is one reason written English so often has to resort to italics or clumsy paraphrase to recover it.

The core observation is that a sentence with fixed words can be pronounced with the main accent in different places, and each placement licenses a different set of questions to which the sentence is a coherent answer. "John gave Mary a BOOK" answers "What did John give Mary?" "John gave MARY a book" answers "Who did John give a book to?" "JOHN gave Mary a book" answers "Who gave Mary a book?" The accented constituent is in focus; the rest is background. Formal work by Mats Rooth in the 1980s and 1990s treats focus as introducing a set of alternatives, so that focusing "book" evokes the set of things John might have given Mary and asserts that the book is the one.

The complementary phenomenon is deaccenting. English systematically strips pitch accents from material that is already given in the discourse. If someone says "I need a screwdriver", the reply "I don't have a screwdriver" places the main accent on "have", not on "screwdriver", because the screwdriver is now given. Failing to deaccent given material is one of the most audible markers of non-native English and of certain speech synthesis systems, and it makes speech sound oddly emphatic or robotic even when every segment is correct.

Contrastive focus goes further, typically using a sharper accent, often L+H* in the AM notation, with a wider pitch excursion and greater duration. "I said the RED one, not the blue one" carries an unmistakable contrastive contour. Second-occurrence focus, where a focused item is repeated, is realised with duration and intensity but usually without a pitch accent, which was an important empirical discovery because it shows that focus marking and pitch accenting are separable.

Languages differ profoundly in how they mark focus. English and German rely almost entirely on prosody, keeping word order relatively fixed. Hungarian, Russian and Turkish move focused constituents to a dedicated syntactic position. Japanese uses particles and a prosodic effect in which focus triggers post-focal compression, dramatically flattening the pitch range of everything after the focused item. Many Bantu languages use a dedicated verbal morphology. Because of this, a learner of English whose first language marks focus syntactically must learn not just new tunes but a whole new division of labour between syntax and prosody, and this is a persistent difficulty well into advanced proficiency.

The default, unmarked case is called broad focus or neutral accentuation, where the accent falls on the last lexical item of the phrase by a rule sometimes called the Nuclear Stress Rule. Everything else is a deviation from that default, and the deviation is what carries the message.

sections.heading: Boundary Tones, Questions and the Meanings of Melody
sections.body:
The endings of phrases carry a disproportionate share of intonational meaning, and the near-universal association of rising pitch with questioning is one of the few genuinely cross-linguistic prosodic tendencies. It is nonetheless a tendency rather than a law, and the exceptions are instructive.

In English, polar (yes-no) questions typically end in a rise: "Are you coming?" ends L* H-H%. Wh-questions, by contrast, typically end in a fall, the same H* L-L% as a declarative: "Where are you going?" spoken with a rise sounds either echoic or surprised. This split is common but not universal. Hungarian yes-no questions use a distinctive rise-fall on the penultimate syllable. Belfast English and several other varieties use rises on declaratives so pervasively that the question-statement distinction is carried elsewhere. Chickasaw, remarkably, uses a falling contour for questions and a rising one for statements, the reverse of the supposed universal.

Where a rise-for-questions tendency does exist, the usual functional explanation, associated with Dwight Bolinger and later with the frequency code proposed by John Ohala, is that high and rising pitch is iconically associated with smallness, submission, deference and non-finality, while low and falling pitch is associated with size, dominance and finality. The frequency code is grounded in a real physical fact — larger larynges produce lower frequencies — and it plausibly explains why rising terminals correlate with politeness and question-hood across many unrelated languages. It is a plausible functional account, not a proven mechanism, and it does not explain the counterexamples.

Terminal rises on declaratives, variously called uptalk, high rising terminal or Australian Question Intonation, have spread widely in Australian, New Zealand, Californian and increasingly British English since at least the 1960s. Popular commentary treats them as marks of insecurity, especially when produced by young women. The research picture is different: sociolinguistic work by Cynthia McLemore and others suggests HRT functions largely as a floor-holding and listener-checking device, signalling that the speaker has more to say and is monitoring uptake, and its use by men is systematically underreported by listeners who have already decided what it means.

Beyond questions, boundary tones distinguish finality from continuation. A list read with a falling terminal on every item sounds like a series of separate assertions; read with rises on all but the last it sounds like a coherent list, and the final fall is what signals the list is complete. Speakers use this so automatically that interruption of a non-final rise feels distinctly rude, and telephone conversations are managed in large part through these cues, since no visual channel is available. Plateau or level terminals are used in English for the routine and the read-aloud, which is why announcements at railway stations sound characteristically flat.

sections.heading: Emotion, Attitude and Sociolinguistic Variation in the Voice
sections.body:
Beyond grammar, prosody carries who the speaker is and how they feel, and it does so with enough reliability that listeners make consequential judgements from a few seconds of speech.

Emotional prosody has been studied systematically since Klaus Scherer's work from the 1970s onward, and the findings are reasonably consistent across languages. Anger raises mean F0 and intensity, widens pitch range, speeds articulation rate and increases high-frequency energy through tenser phonation. Sadness lowers mean F0, narrows range, slows rate to as little as 3 syllables per second and often adds breathiness. Fear raises F0 sharply and irregularly with a fast, ragged rate. Joy raises F0 and rate with a wide range but a less pressed voice quality than anger. Recognition accuracy for these basic categories in forced-choice tasks typically runs 55 to 70 per cent against a chance rate of 20 to 25 per cent, and cross-cultural recognition is above chance but consistently lower than within-culture recognition — an in-group advantage of roughly 10 to 15 percentage points. This is real but not enormous, and it argues for a partly universal, partly learned system.

Attitudinal prosody is more language-specific than emotional prosody, and it is where second-language speakers most often go wrong without knowing it. Politeness in English tends to use a wider pitch range, higher onsets and more rise-terminal patterns; a flat, narrow-range delivery of a polite formula reads as insincere or bored. In Japanese, politeness is signalled partly by pitch range but heavily by morphology, so a Japanese speaker of English may produce grammatically impeccable polite forms with prosody that sounds curt, while an English speaker of Japanese may sound cloying by overusing pitch range where the language does not require it.

Sociolinguistic prosodic variables are numerous and change over time. Creaky voice at phrase ends has become highly salient in American English and, like uptalk, attracts a volume of negative commentary out of all proportion to its communicative consequence; it is common in both sexes and in many other languages including Danish and Finnish, where it goes unremarked. Regional intonation differences are large: Northern Irish and Glaswegian English use rising nuclear tones where southern British English uses falls, so that a routine Belfast statement can be heard as a question by an outsider, with real consequences for how speakers are judged in interviews and courtrooms.

Speaking rate, pausing behaviour and pitch range also vary by register in systematic ways: sports commentary and auctioneering compress rate and widen range; news reading uses characteristic level terminals and step-down patterns; religious and ceremonial registers in many cultures adopt a chant-like restricted range. Listeners identify register from a few seconds of prosody with high accuracy even in a language they do not speak, which shows how much of it is carried by the melody alone.

sections.heading: How Children Acquire Prosody
sections.body:
Prosody is the earliest part of language a child masters, and it is mastered before a single word is understood. This makes acquisition evidence unusually informative about what prosody is for.

Hearing begins in utero at roughly 24 to 28 weeks of gestation, and the uterine wall acts as a low-pass filter, attenuating frequencies above about 1000 Hz. What reaches the fetus is therefore the prosodic envelope of the mother's speech with the segmental detail stripped out. Newborns just hours old prefer their mother's voice to a stranger's, prefer their native language to a rhythmically different one, and can discriminate languages from different rhythm classes even when the speech is synthesised to remove all segmental cues. Jacques Mehler and colleagues demonstrated the language-discrimination effect in four-day-olds in 1988.

Infant-directed speech, the register adults spontaneously adopt with babies, is prosodically extreme: pitch is raised by 2 to 3 semitones or more, range is expanded to as much as two octaves, vowels are lengthened, tempo is slowed by roughly a third and contours are exaggerated and repetitive. It appears in a wide range of cultures, though with real variation in degree — some communities, including several documented in Papua New Guinea and among the Quiché Maya, use it much less, and blanket claims of universality overstate the evidence. Infants prefer it strongly, and controlled studies show it aids word segmentation and vowel category learning, so its function is plausibly pedagogical as well as affective.

Prosodic learning proceeds fast. By 6 to 9 months infants show a preference for the dominant stress pattern of their native language: English-learning infants prefer trochaic (strong-weak) word forms, which matches the fact that about 90 per cent of English content words in speech to children begin with a stressed syllable. Peter Jusczyk and colleagues showed infants use this metrical regularity to segment words from continuous speech, a strategy known as the Metrical Segmentation Strategy proposed by Anne Cutler. Infants learning French, which lacks this asymmetry, do not show the preference.

Production follows a parallel path. Babbling from around 6 to 10 months already carries the intonation contours of the ambient language, so that adults can identify the target language of babbling from prosody alone at above-chance rates. The two-word stage shows correct placement of contrastive stress. Full mastery, though, takes years: correct deaccenting of given information is not adult-like until around age 6 to 8 in English, complex focus structures later still, and the sarcastic and ironic uses of prosody are often not reliably comprehended until 8 to 10 years. This late timeline is consistent across studies and is a useful benchmark for clinicians.

Children learning tone languages acquire the tonal contrasts remarkably early, often by 2 to 3 years, well before they have mastered the segmental inventory. Mandarin-learning toddlers reliably produce the four-tone contrast while still substituting consonants, which suggests pitch categories are easier to lay down than fine articulatory targets. The exception is that tone sandhi rules, the automatic changes a tone undergoes next to another tone, take much longer and are still being refined at school age.

sections.heading: Prosodic Disorders and Clinical Assessment
sections.body:
Prosody can break down in isolation from the rest of language, and the pattern of breakdown is diagnostically informative. The umbrella term for impaired prosody is dysprosody, and it takes several distinct forms.

Aprosodia following right-hemisphere damage is the most theoretically interesting. Elliott Ross's work from 1981 onward described patients with right frontal or temporoparietal lesions who retained fluent, grammatical speech but produced it in a flat monotone and could not identify emotion in others' voices. This maps onto a broader lateralisation picture in which linguistic prosody, such as the question-statement distinction and lexical tone, is processed substantially in the left hemisphere alongside the rest of language, while affective prosody depends more on right-hemisphere structures. The dissociation is real but the localisation is less clean than early accounts implied, and current imaging work supports a bilateral network with right-lateralised weighting for slower, pitch-based cues.

Foreign Accent Syndrome is a rare condition, with perhaps a few hundred documented cases since the first description by Pierre Marie in 1907, in which a speaker after stroke or head injury sounds to listeners like a non-native speaker of their own language. The mechanism is not the acquisition of a foreign accent but the loss of fine prosodic and articulatory control, producing changes in vowel quality, timing and stress placement that listeners then interpret through the nearest available accent category.

Parkinson's disease produces hypokinetic dysarthria with a characteristic prosodic signature: reduced loudness, monopitch, monoloudness, short rushes of speech and imprecise consonants. The condition affects roughly 90 per cent of patients over the course of the illness and is a major driver of social withdrawal. Loud-voice therapy programmes, of which the Lee Silverman Voice Treatment is the best-evidenced, target amplitude specifically and produce measurable gains that generalise partly to pitch variability.

Prosodic atypicality is one of the most consistently reported features of autistic speech, described in the earliest clinical accounts by Leo Kanner in 1943 and confirmed repeatedly since. Reported features include unusual pitch range, atypical stress placement, and difficulty with the pragmatic use of prosody such as deaccenting given information. It is important to state plainly that the evidence base is uneven, that many findings do not replicate, that "atypical" is defined against a neurotypical norm rather than against any functional standard, and that intelligibility is generally unaffected.

Congenital and acquired hearing loss produces a distinctive prosodic profile, because pitch is the acoustic dimension that cochlear implants transmit worst. Current implant processing strategies deliver envelope information well and fine temporal structure poorly, so implanted listeners typically perform near chance on intonation-based question identification and on lexical tone in tone languages, even when word recognition in quiet is excellent. This is one of the clearest demonstrations that prosody and segments are carried by partly separate acoustic channels.

Clinical assessment tools include the Profiling Elements of Prosodic Systems in Children (PEPS-C), which tests reception and production of turn-end, affect, chunking and focus separately, and the Aprosodia Battery for adults. The design principle in both is to separate perception from production and linguistic from affective function, because the four combinations dissociate and treatment differs accordingly.

sections.heading: Measuring Prosody: Instruments, Procedure and What Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Prosodic analysis is unusually vulnerable to measurement error, because the most important variable — fundamental frequency — is estimated by algorithms that fail in specific, predictable ways. Anyone working with prosodic data needs to know the failure modes, because a plausible-looking contour can be entirely an artefact.

The standard free tool is Praat, written by Paul Boersma and David Weenink at the University of Amsterdam and continuously maintained since 1992; it is the de facto standard in phonetics and does pitch tracking, spectrograms, formant analysis, annotation in TextGrids and scripting. Alternatives include the ProsodyPro Praat script suite by Yi Xu for automated large-scale extraction, and Python libraries such as Parselmouth, which wraps Praat, and librosa for signal-level work.
ingredients: A recording made with a head-mounted or lapel microphone at a constant 10 to 20 cm mouth distance; distance changes destroy intensity measurements
Uncompressed audio at 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz sampling and 16-bit depth or better; MP3 and other lossy codecs corrupt the low-amplitude detail that pitch trackers rely on
A quiet room with reverberation time under about 0.5 seconds, or an accepted noise floor at least 30 dB below the speech level
Praat, or an equivalent analysis package, plus a text editor for scripting batch extraction
A written annotation protocol agreed before any labelling begins, so that boundaries and accents are defined the same way by every transcriber
At least two trained labellers for a subset of the data, so inter-transcriber agreement can be reported as a kappa statistic
steps: Record with the microphone fixed relative to the mouth and the gain set so that peaks reach roughly minus 6 dB full scale, leaving headroom without clipping.

Set the pitch analysis floor and ceiling to values appropriate to the speaker before extracting anything: roughly 60 to 300 Hz for a typical adult male voice and 100 to 500 Hz for a typical adult female voice. Leaving the defaults in place is the single commonest cause of octave errors.

Extract the pitch track and inspect it visually against the spectrogram. Look specifically for octave jumps, where the algorithm doubles or halves the true value, and for spurious values during creaky voice, whispered segments and voiceless consonants.
Hand-correct or exclude unreliable frames rather than filtering blindly; a median filter hides errors without fixing them.

Segment the utterance into the units you intend to analyse, normally syllables or vocalic and consonantal intervals, using both the waveform and the spectrogram, and apply a written criterion for every boundary type.
Convert F0 to semitones relative to a speaker-specific baseline before comparing across speakers, since raw hertz comparisons between a 110 Hz and a 210 Hz speaker are meaningless.
Normalise durations for speech rate, using either z-scores within speaker or a rate-normalised metric such as nPVI, before comparing across recordings.
Report the analysis settings, the exclusion criteria and the inter-labeller agreement alongside the results, because none of the numbers are interpretable without them.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Open Questions and What to Do When Prosody Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Several recurring errors damage work on prosody, in the laboratory, in the language classroom and in speech technology, and they are worth naming explicitly.

The first is treating prosody as decoration. Language teaching has historically spent almost all its effort on segments, on the assumption that getting the vowels right is what produces intelligibility. Intelligibility research points the other way. Studies of second-language comprehensibility consistently find that prosodic errors — wrong word stress above all, then wrong sentence-level accent placement, then wrong phrasing — degrade listener comprehension more severely than most segmental errors. A learner who says a fully correct sequence of English phonemes with stress on the wrong syllable of a polysyllabic word is frequently not understood at all, because English listeners use stress position as a primary lexical access cue. The practical corollary is that a learner with limited study time gets far more return from stress and rhythm work than from perfecting a difficult vowel.

The second is over-reading a single acoustic cue. Prosodic categories are signalled by bundles of cues that trade off against one another. A syllable can be perceived as accented with no pitch movement at all if it is long and full-vowelled enough. Conversely, a large pitch excursion at the very end of an utterance may be a boundary tone rather than an accent. Any analysis that reads accent straight off the pitch track will generate confident nonsense.

The third is the octave error, mentioned in every practical treatment and still the commonest single defect in published pitch data. If a contour shows an implausible leap of exactly one octave, it is almost certainly the tracker, not the speaker.

The fourth is assuming universality. It is tempting to project the intonational meanings of one's own language onto others. Rising equals question is a strong tendency, not a law; wide pitch range equals emotional involvement in many European languages but can read as loss of control in others; a flat delivery is respectful in some communities and rude in others. Cross-cultural miscommunication in service encounters, medical consultations and courtrooms is frequently prosodic rather than lexical, and the participants typically diagnose it as rudeness or evasiveness rather than as a difference in convention. John Gumperz's work on cross-cultural miscommunication documented exactly this in British workplaces where South Asian English speakers' falling intonation on offers was heard by British listeners as brusque.

Several questions remain genuinely open. Whether pitch accent is a real category is unresolved. Whether rhythm classes are discrete or continuous is unresolved. Whether the inventory of English pitch accents is six, four or a continuum of gradient variation is actively contested, with strong arguments on both sides and no decisive experiment yet. The compositional meaning of intonational tunes — what H* means as opposed to L+H*, independent of context — has proved much harder to pin down than the elegance of the AM model suggested, and the field has partly retreated to describing distributions rather than meanings. Anyone reading confident claims in this area should check what evidence sits behind them.

guides.title: Phonetics — The Sounds of Speech
guides.summary: Phonetics is the scientific study of the sounds of human speech: how they are produced, transmitted as sound waves, and heard. This guide surveys articulation, acoustics, perception, transcription in the International Phonetic Alphabet, and how sounds behave in running speech.

sections.heading: What Phonetics Studies
sections.body: Phonetics is the scientific study of the sounds human beings use in spoken language: how those sounds are produced by the organs of the mouth, throat, and lungs, how they travel through the air as vibrations, and how they are received and decoded by the ear and brain. It is one of the oldest and most concrete branches of linguistics, because its object of study can be measured, recorded, and reproduced with instruments. Where much of linguistics deals with abstract structure, phonetics keeps at least one foot in the physical world of acoustics and physiology. The ancient Indian grammarian Panini and his followers described the articulation of Sanskrit sounds with remarkable precision more than two thousand years ago, and the modern discipline took shape in the nineteenth century through the work of Henry Sweet, Alexander Melville Bell, and others. It is essential to distinguish phonetics from phonology, its closest neighbour. Phonetics describes the raw physical facts of speech sounds, the actual measurable events, without regard to which language is being spoken. Phonology, by contrast, studies how a particular language organizes sounds into a system: which differences signal a change of meaning, which patterns are allowed, and how sounds alter one another. The English sounds at the start of pin and spin are phonetically different, since the first is aspirated, released with a puff of air, and the second is not, yet English speakers treat them as the same sound, because the difference never distinguishes two words. Phonetics notices the difference; phonology explains why speakers ignore it. A convention marks this divide. Phonetic transcription, showing precise physical detail, is written between square brackets, so aspirated p appears as a symbol with a small raised h beside it. Phonological representation, showing only the meaning-bearing categories called phonemes, is written between slashes. The same utterance can therefore be transcribed narrowly, with much detail, or broadly, with little. Phonetics matters far beyond the seminar room. It underpins the teaching of pronunciation to language learners, the training of actors and singers, the diagnosis and treatment of speech disorders by speech-language pathologists, the design of speech-recognition and text-to-speech technology, and forensic voice comparison in criminal cases. It also grounds the reconstruction of extinct languages, since sound change follows physically motivated pathways. Because it studies a universal human capacity, for every hearing community that has ever existed has spoken, phonetics offers a window onto what the vocal apparatus can do and what all languages share. The remainder of this guide surveys how sounds are made, classified, transcribed, measured, and perceived, building from the anatomy of production to the acoustics of the signal and the psychology of hearing.

sections.heading: The Three Branches and the Speech Chain
sections.body: Speaking and understanding a single word sets off a chain of events that phoneticians call the speech chain, and the discipline divides into three branches according to which link each studies. The chain begins in the speaker's brain, which assembles a message and issues motor commands to the muscles of respiration and the vocal organs. Those muscles move, shaping a stream of air into a sound. The sound radiates outward as a pressure wave. The wave reaches the listener's ear, is converted into nerve impulses, and travels to the listener's brain, where it is recognized as language. Each link can be observed and measured, and each supports a distinct field of study. Articulatory phonetics studies the first link: how the speech organs move to produce sounds. It asks where in the vocal tract a constriction is made, how the tongue, lips, and soft palate are positioned, whether the vocal folds vibrate, and how the airstream is set in motion. This is the oldest branch, since the movements of the mouth can be felt and, to a degree, seen. Its descriptive vocabulary, terms such as bilabial, velar, fricative, and voiced, furnishes the labels used throughout phonetics and is the foundation of the International Phonetic Alphabet. Acoustic phonetics studies the middle link: the sound wave itself as it travels through the air. Using recordings and computer analysis, it measures the frequencies, amplitudes, and durations that make up the physical signal, and displays them in waveforms and spectrograms. Because the acoustic signal is what actually passes between speaker and listener, acoustic phonetics provides an objective, instrument-based record that can confirm or refine the impressions of the ear. It became a mature field only in the mid-twentieth century, when the sound spectrograph, developed at Bell Laboratories during the 1940s, first made the invisible structure of speech visible. Auditory phonetics studies the final link: how the ear receives the signal and how the brain perceives it as speech. It draws on the anatomy of hearing and on psychoacoustics, the study of how physical properties of sound relate to the sensations of loudness, pitch, and quality. Perception is not a passive mirror of the signal; listeners actively interpret it, filling gaps and resolving ambiguities using knowledge of their language. These branches are complementary rather than rival. A full account of any speech sound describes how it is made, what acoustic pattern it produces, and how that pattern is heard. Historically the branches developed with different tools and different questions, and researchers still specialize, but modern laboratories routinely combine them, correlating tongue movements captured by ultrasound or electromagnetic sensors with the acoustic output and with listeners' judgments. Together they trace the sound from mind to mind.

sections.heading: Airstream Mechanisms and the Vocal Tract
sections.body: Every speech sound requires moving air, and the source of that movement is called an airstream mechanism. The great majority of the world's speech sounds, and all the sounds of English, use the pulmonic egressive airstream: the lungs push air outward, driven by the elastic recoil of the rib cage and the controlled contraction of the muscles of respiration, especially the diaphragm and the intercostals. Because ordinary breathing already supplies this outward flow, it is the most efficient basis for speech, and no known language lacks pulmonic egressive sounds. Three other mechanisms occur in the world's languages. Glottalic sounds use the larynx as a piston. When the closed vocal folds are jerked upward, they compress the air above them and produce ejectives, sharp sounds common in the languages of the Caucasus, the Americas, and parts of Africa. When the larynx is pulled downward with the folds nearly closed, air is briefly sucked inward, producing implosives, heard in Sindhi, Zulu, and many other languages. Velaric sounds, made by trapping air between two closures in the mouth and expanding the cavity, produce clicks, the sounds written in English as tut-tut or a giddy-up signal to a horse, but used as ordinary consonants in the Khoisan languages and in Zulu and Xhosa. These non-pulmonic sounds show the range of what the vocal tract can do beyond simple breathing. The vocal tract is the passage above the larynx through which the airstream is shaped, and it is conventionally divided into cavities and articulators. The pharynx is the tube at the back of the throat; above it the airway splits, with the oral cavity leading to the lips and the nasal cavity branching off through the nose. The velum, or soft palate, is a movable flap at the back of the roof of the mouth; when it is raised it seals off the nose so that air escapes only through the mouth, and when it is lowered air passes through the nose, giving nasal sounds such as m and n. Within the mouth, the articulators are the organs that move and the surfaces they move toward. The lower lip and, above all, the tongue are the active articulators, capable of forming constrictions at many points. The tongue is conventionally divided into the tip, the blade just behind it, the front, the back, and the root. The passive articulators are the relatively fixed surfaces they approach: the upper lip, the upper teeth, the bony alveolar ridge behind them, the hard palate, the soft palate, and the pharyngeal wall. By bringing an active articulator toward a passive one, a speaker narrows the tract at a chosen place, and the size and shape of the resulting cavities determine the sound. This anatomy is the stage on which all articulation is performed.

sections.heading: Voicing and Phonation
sections.body: Before the airstream reaches the mouth it passes through the larynx, a cartilaginous structure in the throat that houses the vocal folds, two bands of muscle and tissue often loosely called the vocal cords. The gap between them is the glottis. The behaviour of the vocal folds is one of the most important variables in speech, because it determines whether a sound is voiced or voiceless and, more broadly, its phonation type.
